A call without await doesn't postpone anything. Remember the state machine (section 3): builder.Start runs the first MoveNext right away. Step by step for the loop below:

  • 1. SaveAsync(o) runs synchronously, on the loop's thread, up to the first await that really waits: the database request has gone out.
  • 2. The method returns an unfinished task. Nobody kept it, so the reference is lost.
  • 3. The loop immediately calls the next SaveAsync without waiting for the first. All the saves run at the same time, even though the code looks sequential.
  • 4. LogAsync writes "saved" while the saves are still running or have already failed.

If the saves share one connection or one DbContext (EF Core), it's also a race. The second call starts an operation before the first one has finished, and EF Core throws InvalidOperationException ("A second operation was started on this context instance…").

cards.q: Where is the missing await?
cards.explain: SaveAsync is called, but nobody waits for its task: the loop moves on, the saves run all at once, and their errors are lost. Write await SaveAsync(o) to save one by one, or collect the tasks and await Task.WhenAll to save them together.

cards.q: What ends up in the log?
options: "saved", even though the saves are still running or have already failed
Nothing: LogAsync won't be called while the saves are running
The log entry appears after all the saves
cards.explain: Each SaveAsync call returned at its first pause, and the loop moved on. LogAsync knows nothing about the saves: their tasks were thrown away.

wrong.1: A call without await doesn't stop the method: LogAsync runs right after the loop.
wrong.2: That would happen with await in the loop or with await Task.WhenAll. Here nobody waits for the SaveAsync tasks.

cards.q: SaveAsync saves an order through a shared DbContext (EF Core) and waits for the database. The loop calls it without await for three orders. Where does InvalidOperationException "A second operation was started on this context…" show up?
cards.code:
foreach (var o in orders)   // three orders
    SaveAsync(o);           // inside: await _db.SaveChangesAsync()
options: Inside the later SaveAsync calls: the exception lands in their tasks, which nobody awaits
It's thrown out of the foreach loop on the second call
Nowhere: without await the calls run one after another
cards.explain: The first SaveAsync reached the await on the request and returned, but its operation on the context is still running. The next call starts a new operation on the same context, and EF Core throws. The exception is thrown inside an async method, so it lands in the task (section 2) instead of escaping the call. Nobody awaits the task, so nobody sees the error.

wrong.1: An async method's exception never escapes the call, even one thrown before the first await: it lands in the task.
wrong.2: Without await the loop doesn't wait: the next call starts while the previous one sits at its await.

cards.title: What gets lost: the error and the lifetime
cards.body:
The error. Each SaveAsync's exception sits in its task (section 2). Nobody awaits the task, so nobody rethrows the exception. UnobservedTaskException fires only when the GC collects the task, and that may never happen.

The lifetime. A task runs until it's done, and it doesn't care whether whoever started it is still alive. The object that created it is no longer needed, the HTTP request has already been answered, and the task is still running. In ASP.NET Core the request's services, such as the DbContext, are destroyed after the response. A task that uses them gets ObjectDisposedException, and nobody sees that either.

The process. In a console app and on a server, continuations run on pool threads, and those are background threads: the process doesn't wait for them. A console program that has returned from Main cuts an unfinished task off mid-sentence.

cards.q: What's wrong with fire-and-forget? Select all that apply.
options: You can't tell when the task finished
Nobody sees its exception
The task can outlive the object or request that started it
Calls in a loop run at the same time, even though the code looks sequential
The call itself runs slower than with await
cards.explain: Speed has nothing to do with it: a call without await starts the same way as one with await. The problem is control: nobody waits for the task, nobody sees its error, and nobody tracks how long it lives.

cards.title: async void: where the exception goes
cards.body:
You know the rule from section 2: async void is for event handlers only. Now the mechanism.

An async Task method's builder is AsyncTaskMethodBuilder (section 3): the catch in MoveNext calls SetException, and the exception waits in the task. async void has no task, so the compiler uses a different builder, AsyncVoidMethodBuilder. When it's created, it remembers SynchronizationContext.Current. When MoveNext catches an exception (before the first await or after, it doesn't matter), there's nowhere to put it, so the builder throws it again:

  • there was a context (WPF, WinForms, Unity): context.Post(() => throw e). The exception flies out of the main thread's queue, where none of your try blocks are. What happens next is up to the framework; more on that below;
  • there was no context (console, ASP.NET Core, a pool thread): the exception is thrown on a pool thread. An unhandled exception on the pool terminates the process, and on a server that's the whole server with every request.

A try around the call won't help. The call returned at the first pause, and if the exception happened before it, the catch inside MoveNext has already taken it.
cards.deep: AsyncVoidMethodBuilder also tells the context when the method starts and ends (OperationStarted and OperationCompleted). Contexts that wait for every async void are built on this, for example in test frameworks.

cards.q: A console program. What happens?
options: After 100 ms the process crashes with an unhandled InvalidOperationException
It prints "caught"
The exception quietly stays in Fire's task, and the program keeps waiting for input
cards.explain: Fire returned at the await, and the try was over. 100 ms later the continuation throws on a pool thread. A console app has no context, so AsyncVoidMethodBuilder throws the exception on a pool thread. An unhandled exception on the pool terminates the process, and ReadLine can't hold it back.

wrong.1: By the time of the exception Fire returned long ago, and the try is behind us.
wrong.2: async void has no task, so the exception has nowhere to land. It's an unawaited async Task whose exception gets quietly lost.

cards.q: Same program, but Fire throws before its first await. Will the catch get it?
options: No: the catch inside MoveNext took the exception, the builder threw it on a pool thread, and the process crashes
Yes: up to the first await the method runs synchronously on the caller's thread
Yes, but only in a console app, which has no context
cards.explain: The first MoveNext does run synchronously, inside the call. But the method body is wrapped in the generated code's try/catch (section 3). That catch hands the exception to the builder, and AsyncVoidMethodBuilder with no context throws it on the pool. Nothing escapes the Fire call.

wrong.1: Synchronously, yes, but the exception is caught by the catch inside MoveNext, not by your try.
wrong.2: The opposite: a console app has no context, so the exception is thrown on a pool thread and crashes the process.

cards.title: async void in WPF, WinForms and Unity
cards.body:
An exception the builder sent through Post runs as an ordinary item in the main thread's queue. None of your try blocks are on that path, so the framework decides what happens next:

  • WPF. The Dispatcher raises Dispatcher.UnhandledException, and Application raises its own Application.DispatcherUnhandledException. If a handler sets e.Handled = true, the app keeps running. If not, the exception escapes the message loop and the process terminates.
  • WinForms. The message loop catches the exception and raises Application.ThreadException. If nobody has subscribed, WinForms shows its standard dialog, "Unhandled exception has occurred in your application", with Continue and Quit buttons. Click Continue, and the app keeps running in an unknown state.
  • Unity. The main thread drains the UnitySynchronizationContext queue once per frame (details in section 6), and the engine logs any exception from it to the console. The game doesn't crash, but the method stops where the error happened.

A global handler is a last line of defense, not error handling: it doesn't know which method failed or how far it got. An async void handler's errors are caught by a try/catch inside it.

cards.q: Unity. What happens when Start reaches the throw?
options: The exception shows up in the console, the game keeps running, and the rest of Start never runs
The process terminates, like a WPF app with no DispatcherUnhandledException handler
The exception quietly stays in Start's task, and nothing appears in the console
cards.explain: In Unity the main thread has a UnitySynchronizationContext, so AsyncVoidMethodBuilder sent the exception through Post. It flew out of the main thread's queue, and Unity logged it to the console. The process is alive, but the enemy is left half set up.

wrong.1: WPF with no handler and a pool thread with no context terminate the process. Unity only logs an exception from its queue to the console.
wrong.2: async void has no task: the builder rethrows the exception, and Unity logs it.

cards.title: If you really must fire and forget
cards.body:
Sometimes there really is no need to wait: an email, a metric, a cache warm-up. Then make sure the error isn't lost and that "not waiting" is visible in the code.

  • A wrapper with try/catch inside. RunSafeAsync awaits the work itself and logs the exception. There's nobody outside to catch the error, so it's caught inside the task. The try covers the synchronous part too: work() is called inside it.
  • Discard: _ = task; This is an assignment to a variable that can't be read. It silences CS4014 and tells the reader: not waiting, on purpose. It does nothing else. The task runs the same way, and without a wrapper its exception is lost the same way.
  • On a server, outside the request. Don't carry HttpContext or the request's services into a background task; copy the data beforehand. Long background work goes to a BackgroundService, a .NET host class with an ExecuteAsync(stoppingToken) method. The host starts it at startup and cancels the token at shutdown. Since .NET 6 an unhandled exception in it stops the host by default instead of vanishing. Details in section 6.

cards.q: What does _ = change in the line _ = SaveAsync(o);?
options: It only silences CS4014 and shows you're not waiting on purpose: SaveAsync's error is still lost
It waits for the task synchronously, like .Wait()
It catches the task's exception and logs it
cards.explain: A discard is a plain assignment to a variable that can't be read. The task starts and lives exactly as it would without it. To keep the error from getting lost, you need a try/catch inside the task, as in RunSafeAsync.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Not waiting on purpose, no warning
Rethrows the exception: to the context or the pool
Where a background job's error is sure to be caught
Host background work outside a request

lessons.title: lock and await
lessons.sub: Why lock doesn't survive await, and how SemaphoreSlim works

cards.title: No await inside lock
cards.body:
The compiler won't allow it: error CS1996. To see why, look at what lock turns into. The compiler expands lock (x) { … } into (simplified) Monitor.Enter(x) and Monitor.Exit(x) in a finally. Monitor remembers the owner thread, and Exit from any other thread throws SynchronizationLockException.

If you get around the rule and call Monitor by hand, the code compiles and breaks:

  • console and server (no context): the continuation after await runs on a pool thread, not the one that took the lock. Its Monitor.Exit throws SynchronizationLockException, and the lock stays with the first thread. Any other thread that comes to this lock will wait forever;
  • WPF and WinForms (there is a context): the continuation comes back to the same UI thread, and Exit succeeds. But while the await is pending, the UI thread processes its queue, and a second click walks into the "taken" lock. Monitor is reentrant: the owner thread enters again without waiting. The lock protects nothing.
cards.deep: The exact expansion is Monitor.Enter(x, ref lockTaken) inside the try and if (lockTaken) Monitor.Exit(x) in the finally. Since C# 13 and .NET 9, lock on an object of type System.Threading.Lock expands into Lock.EnterScope(), but the rule is the same: the lock belongs to a thread, and CS1996 still applies.

cards.q: Why can't you await inside a lock?
options: The lock belongs to a thread, and after await the method may continue on another thread
await inside a lock is too slow
lock can't work with Task objects
cards.explain: lock is Monitor.Enter and Monitor.Exit, and only the owner thread can release a Monitor. After await the continuation may run on another pool thread, and Exit from there throws SynchronizationLockException.

cards.q: A console app's async Main gets around CS1996 and calls Monitor by hand. What happens at Monitor.Exit?
options: SynchronizationLockException: Exit is called by a pool thread that never took the lock
Nothing: a Monitor can be released from any thread
Deadlock: Exit waits until the owner thread releases the lock
cards.explain: The main thread called Enter. A console app has no context, so the continuation after Task.Delay runs on a pool thread. Monitor checks the owner and throws, and the lock stays with the main thread.

wrong.1: Monitor remembers its owner thread and can be released only by it.
wrong.2: Exit doesn't wait for anything: it checks the owner and throws right away.

cards.q: WPF: the same hand-written Monitor around an await in a click handler. While the first SaveAsync waits for the database, the user clicks again. What happens?
options: The second handler gets in: the UI thread already owns the lock, and Monitor is reentrant
The second click waits until the first handler leaves the lock
SynchronizationLockException on the second Monitor.Enter
cards.explain: One UI thread runs both handlers. While the first one sits at its await, the thread processes the queue and runs the second handler. Monitor sees the owner and just bumps its entry count. Two saves run at the same time, even though the lock is "taken".

wrong.1: The owner enters without waiting. And if Enter did wait, it would block the UI thread, which still has to run the first handler's continuation.
wrong.2: An owner entering again isn't an error: Monitor is reentrant.

cards.title: SemaphoreSlim: an async lock
cards.body:
SemaphoreSlim has no owner, only a count of free slots. The constructor SemaphoreSlim(initialCount, maxCount) takes how many slots are free now and how many there can be at most. (1, 1) is an async lock for one; (3, 3) lets up to three in at once.

  • WaitAsync(): if the count is above zero, it decrements it and returns an already completed task. The await takes the fast path, with no pause (section 3).
  • If the count is zero, it puts you in the queue of waiters and returns an unfinished task. The method stops at the await, and the thread is free.
  • Release(): if someone is waiting, it completes the task of one of the waiters, and the slot passes to them. Which one isn't guaranteed: no order, not even FIFO, is promised. If nobody is waiting, it increments the count. Releasing beyond maxCount throws SemaphoreFullException.

There's no owner, so you can release from any thread, after await too. WaitAsync has an overload with a token: WaitAsync(ct). If it's canceled, it throws OperationCanceledException, and you didn't get a slot. That's why WaitAsync goes before the try: the Release in finally must give back only the slot you took.

cards.q: Build an async lock
cards.explain: The semaphore has Wait() too, but it blocks the thread until a slot is free. Enter is a Monitor method; SemaphoreSlim doesn't have it.

cards.q: What does new SemaphoreSlim(3, 3) mean?
options: 3 free slots out of 3: up to three get in at once
One can be inside, and three more wait in the queue
Three attempts to get in, then an exception
cards.explain: The first number is how many slots are free now, the second is the maximum. Each WaitAsync takes a slot, each Release gives one back. This is how you limit concurrency, for example the number of simultaneous requests to an API.

cards.q: SemaphoreSlim(3, 3), all three slots are taken. What happens on a fourth await _gate.WaitAsync()?
options: WaitAsync returns an unfinished task: the method stops at the await, and the thread is free until someone calls Release
The thread blocks until someone calls Release
WaitAsync throws: there are no slots
cards.explain: The count is zero, so the caller joins the queue of waiters. Release will hand the slot to it: it completes its task, and the method continues after the await.

cards.title: The semaphore isn't reentrant
cards.body:
Monitor's owner gets in the way of async code. SemaphoreSlim has no owner, and that has a price too: the semaphore doesn't know that "it's you again". Entering the same semaphore again from the same call chain is a silent deadlock. No exception, the task just never completes.

  • 1. SaveAsync takes the only slot; the count is 0.
  • 2. Inside, SaveAsync awaits FlushAsync, which also calls WaitAsync on _gate. There's no slot, so FlushAsync joins the queue.
  • 3. Only the Release in SaveAsync's finally gives the slot back. But SaveAsync is waiting for FlushAsync. Each waits for the other.

The fix is not to take the lock twice. The inner method works without the lock (it's often called …Core), and only the outer one takes it.

cards.q: _gate = new SemaphoreSlim(1, 1). What happens when RefreshAsync is called?
options: RefreshAsync hangs forever: GetAsync waits for a slot that only RefreshAsync itself will give back
It works: the same call chain is already inside, as with Monitor
GetAsync throws SemaphoreFullException
cards.explain: The semaphore has no owner, so it doesn't know GetAsync was called from inside the lock. The count is 0, GetAsync joins the queue, and RefreshAsync waits for GetAsync. Nobody ever reaches Release.

wrong.1: That's Monitor's reentrancy. SemaphoreSlim counts slots, not threads or calls.
wrong.2: SemaphoreFullException comes from an extra Release, and here nobody reaches Release at all.

cards.q: Why does WaitAsync(ct) go before the try rather than as the first line inside it?
options: If the wait is canceled, finally releases a slot you never took, and an extra caller gets in
Inside a try, WaitAsync blocks the thread
Inside a try it doesn't compile
cards.explain: On cancellation WaitAsync(ct) throws OperationCanceledException, and no slot was taken. But finally still calls Release: a slot frees up while its owner is still inside, and someone else gets in. Later an extra Release hits the maximum and throws SemaphoreFullException.

cards.q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
options: WaitAsync doesn't block the thread while it waits for a slot
SemaphoreSlim can be released from a different thread
A second WaitAsync from the same call chain gets in, like re-entering a Monitor
Monitor.Exit can be called from any thread
You can skip Release: the GC will give the slot back
cards.explain: The semaphore has no owner: you can release it from anywhere, but it also won't recognize "your" repeated entry. Monitor, on the contrary, remembers its owner and can be released only by it. Nobody will give a semaphore slot back for you.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Monitor: the lock belongs to a thread
Wait for a slot without blocking the thread

lessons.title: TaskCompletionSource
lessons.sub: Your own task from callbacks: completion, unsubscribing, cancellation and continuations

cards.title: A task you complete yourself
cards.body:
TaskCompletionSource<T> creates a Task<T> with no body. Nobody runs it, and no thread waits on it. You complete the task yourself, from the outside, in one of three ways, one per final state (section 1):

  • SetResult(x): success with a result;
  • SetException(e): an error (Faulted), await will throw e;
  • SetCanceled(): cancellation (Canceled), await will throw OperationCanceledException.

This is how an old callback- or event-based API becomes a task you can await. Step by step:

  • 1. GetLocationAsync subscribes to the events, starts the GPS and immediately returns the unfinished tcs.Task.
  • 2. The caller awaits: the task isn't ready, so the method registers its continuation and returns. The thread is free while the GPS looks for satellites.
  • 3. The GPS library raises OnFix on its own thread, and the handler calls SetResult.
  • 4. The task is complete, and the caller's continuation starts. Exactly where is the main catch of this lesson; more on it below.

cards.q: What does tcs.SetResult(loc) do?
options: Completes tcs.Task with a result, and everyone awaiting it continues
Starts the GPS search
Blocks the thread until someone takes the result
cards.explain: A TaskCompletionSource task doesn't run anything itself: it's completed from the outside. SetResult moves it to a final state and starts the continuations of whoever is waiting.

cards.q: Which line can leave the task hanging forever?
cards.explain: On an error the handler only logs it, and nobody completes the task: the await will wait forever. You need tcs.SetException(e).

cards.title: Complete exactly once
cards.body:
A task completes once. A second SetResult, SetException or SetCanceled throws InvalidOperationException ("An attempt was made to transition a task to a final state when it had already completed"). Each has a Try version: TrySetResult, TrySetException, TrySetCanceled. If the task is already complete, the Try version does nothing and returns false.

There are usually several sources of completion: a success event, an error event, cancellation. They can fire almost at once or more than once: a GPS may well send OnFix twice. The first one wins, and the other Try calls quietly return false. That's why code like this uses only the Try versions.

The code below has three sources: OnFix, OnError and cancellation by token. How the unsubscribing and the cancellation work is in the card after the question.

cards.q: Why does GetLocationAsync(ct) use TrySetResult rather than SetResult?
options: The event may arrive twice or after cancellation: SetResult on a completed task throws InvalidOperationException, while TrySetResult returns false
TrySetResult waits until the task is ready to accept a result, while SetResult throws right away
SetResult can be called only from the thread that created the task
cards.explain: A task completes once. With several sources of completion, the first one wins, and the other Try calls quietly return false. A second SetResult would throw right on the library's thread, inside its event handler.

cards.title: Clean up after yourself: unsubscribing and cancellation
cards.body:
Besides the Try versions, GetLocationAsync(ct) has two more duties:

  • Unsubscribe from the events. Otherwise the source holds the handlers, and through them tcs, forever. Every call adds more of them, and all of them fire on every event. The unsubscribing sits in a finally: it runs whatever the await ends with.
  • Hook up cancellation. ct.Register(callback) subscribes a callback to the token's cancellation: Cancel() calls the subscribers (section 2). If the token is already canceled, Register calls the callback right away. The callback completes the task with TrySetCanceled(ct). Register returns a registration, and using removes the subscription when the method ends. A timeout is the same token, just from a CancellationTokenSource with a timeout.

Every path step by step is in the code below.

cards.q: In GetLocationAsync(ct) the token is canceled before OnFix arrives. What does the caller get?
options: await throws OperationCanceledException: Cancel called the Register callback, and it called TrySetCanceled
The task keeps waiting for OnFix: a token only affects methods that accept it
await returns default(Location)
cards.explain: Register subscribed a callback to cancellation. Cancel calls the subscribers, the callback moves the task to Canceled, and await throws OperationCanceledException (more precisely, its subclass TaskCanceledException). finally unsubscribes the events, and using removes the registration.

wrong.1: Without Register that's what would happen: the TaskCompletionSource task knows nothing about the token. Register is exactly what connects it to cancellation.
wrong.2: A canceled task has no value to return: await throws.

cards.q: The finally with the unsubscribing was removed from GetLocationAsync(ct), and the method is called on every screen. What happens after a hundred calls?
options: gps accumulates a hundred pairs of handlers: each holds its own tcs, and all of them fire on every event
Every new call throws InvalidOperationException
New tasks stop completing
cards.explain: A subscription is a reference from gps to the handler, and through it to tcs and everything it captured. Without unsubscribing, the GC can't collect them. The old handlers call TrySetResult on long-completed tasks and get false: no errors you can see, just a leak and extra work on every event.

wrong.1: The old handlers call the Try versions, and on a completed task those return false instead of throwing. SetResult would throw, right inside the library's event handler.
wrong.2: A new call subscribes its own handlers, and the very first event completes its task.

cards.title: The catch: continuations run inside SetResult
cards.body:
Remember section 4: with no context, a continuation usually runs synchronously on the thread that completed the task. A TaskCompletionSource task is completed by your SetResult. So the waiting method's continuation (its MoveNext) runs right inside SetResult, on the thread that called it. SetResult returns only when that method reaches its next real pause or its end.

  • The waiter captured a UI context, and SetResult was called from another thread: the continuation goes via Post to the UI thread's queue, and SetResult returns right away.
  • The waiter has no context (console, ASP.NET Core, a pool thread, ConfigureAwait(false)): the continuation runs right there, inside SetResult.

Why this is dangerous: someone else's code runs on the library's thread and under its locks. While it runs, the library is stuck. If it calls into the library again, it re-enters the library's lock (Monitor is reentrant, previous lesson) while the library's state is half-done. If it synchronously waits for something that needs that lock on another thread, you get a deadlock.

The flag from the GetLocationAsync(ct) code turns this off; more on it after the question.

cards.q: ASP.NET Core, a TaskCompletionSource created without the flag. The library calls SetResult on its own thread under its own lock. Where and when does the request's code after await tcs.Task run?
options: Right away, inside SetResult: on the library's thread and under its lock
On a pool thread, after SetResult returns
On the request's thread, which has been waiting for the task all along
cards.explain: ASP.NET Core has no context, and there's no flag either. The continuation runs synchronously on the thread that completed the task: the library's thread, inside its lock.

wrong.1: That's what would happen with the RunContinuationsAsynchronously flag.
wrong.2: No thread was waiting for the task: the method returned at the await, and the thread went off to serve other requests.

cards.title: RunContinuationsAsynchronously and the naming trap
cards.body:
The TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously flag in the constructor changes step 3 from the previous card: continuations don't run inside SetResult but are queued (to the pool or via Post to the captured context), and SetResult returns right away. The waiter's code runs on another thread, outside the library's locks. Use it by default for TaskCompletionSource: the price is one extra hop through a queue.

A naming trap: the TaskContinuationOptions enum has a member with the same name. new TaskCompletionSource<T>(TaskContinuationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously) compiles because the value goes to the overload with an object state parameter, and it turns nothing on. The CA2247 analyzer warns about this.

cards.q: The flag is there, but continuations still run inside TrySetResult. Which line is to blame?
cards.explain: TaskCompletionSource has no overload that takes TaskContinuationOptions: the value silently goes to the object state parameter. You need TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously. This is exactly what the CA2247 analyzer catches.

cards.q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
options: A second SetResult throws InvalidOperationException
TrySetResult on a completed task returns false
A TaskCompletionSource task has no body: it's completed from the outside
Dispose on a TaskCompletionSource cancels the task
RunContinuationsAsynchronously runs the task on a separate thread
cards.explain: TaskCompletionSource has no Dispose at all: you cancel through SetCanceled or TrySetCanceled. And the flag only affects where the waiters' continuations run: there's nobody to run the task itself.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: A task with no body that you complete yourself
Complete it if it isn't complete yet
Call a callback when the token is canceled

lessons.title: Async streams and await using
lessons.sub: await foreach, generators, cancellation and DisposeAsync

cards.title: Data as it arrives
cards.body:
IAsyncEnumerable<T> is an asynchronous sequence: items arrive one at a time, and you can wait between them. A method with async and yield return is called an async generator. The compiler accepts such a method only if it's declared as IAsyncEnumerable<T> (or IAsyncEnumerator<T>). With Task<List<T>> it's a compile error.

You read the sequence with await foreach. It waits for each next item the same way await waits for a task: while there's no item, the thread is free.

Unlike Task<List<T>>, you can process the first items right away, and you don't have to hold the whole list in memory.

cards.q: Why is IAsyncEnumerable<T> better than Task<List<T>>?
options: You can process the first items without waiting for all of them to load
It's always faster
It doesn't use memory
cards.explain: You don't have to keep a million lines from a file in memory at once: each one is processed while the next is being read.

cards.q: Read an async sequence
cards.code:
___ ___ (var o in ReadOrdersAsync())
    Handle(o);
cards.explain: await foreach waits for each next item without blocking the thread.

cards.title: How await foreach pulls items
cards.body:
A generator is a state machine too (section 3), only it pauses not just at await but also at yield return. The compiler expands await foreach roughly as in the code below. Step by step:

  • 1. Calling ReadOrdersAsync() only creates an object. The generator's body hasn't run yet, and not a single line of the file has been read.
  • 2. The first MoveNextAsync starts the body and runs it to the first yield return. There may be awaits on the way: then MoveNextAsync returns an unfinished ValueTask<bool>, and the consumer waits with no thread.
  • 3. At yield return, MoveNextAsync completes with true, and the item is in Current. The generator stays parked at that yield.
  • 4. The next MoveNextAsync resumes the body after the yield, up to the next yield.
  • 5. The body is done: MoveNextAsync returns false, and the loop exits.
  • 6. DisposeAsync runs the generator's finally (that's where the file is closed), even if you left the loop with break or an exception.

Until the consumer asks for the next item, the generator stays put. That's built-in backpressure: a slow consumer won't let the generator run ahead and fill up memory.

cards.q: var orders = ReadOrdersAsync(); and nothing else. How many lines of the file have been read?
options: None: the generator's body starts running on the first MoveNextAsync
The whole file: an async method runs synchronously up to the first await
One: the generator runs up to the first yield return
cards.explain: Calling a generator only creates the sequence object. The body is started by the first MoveNextAsync, and await foreach is what calls it. That's the difference from an ordinary async method, which runs its first MoveNext right away.

wrong.1: That's how an async Task method behaves: builder.Start runs the first MoveNext immediately. A generator waits until someone asks it for an item.
wrong.2: The body reaches the first yield only on the first MoveNextAsync, and nobody has called it yet.

cards.q: The consumer leaves await foreach with break after three orders. What happens to the finally inside the generator, where the file is closed?
options: It runs right away: await foreach calls DisposeAsync, and that runs the generator's finally
It runs when the GC collects the enumerator
The generator first reads the rest of the file, then runs the finally
cards.explain: await foreach expands into a try/finally with await e.DisposeAsync(). Leaving the loop by any route calls DisposeAsync, and that runs the generator's finally from the yield where it was parked. The rest of the file isn't read.

cards.title: Cancellation in an async stream
cards.body:
You can pass a token to a generator as an ordinary parameter: ReadOrdersAsync(ct). But often one piece of code creates the sequence and another iterates it. Then the consumer passes the token with .WithCancellation(ct).

  • WithCancellation doesn't call the method again and doesn't touch its parameters. The token goes to GetAsyncEnumerator(ct).
  • The enumerator the compiler generated puts that token into the parameter marked with the [EnumeratorCancellation] attribute. If a token was passed both to the parameter and through WithCancellation, they're combined: canceling either one stops the generator.
  • Without the attribute, the token from WithCancellation has nowhere to go, and cancellation silently doesn't work. The compiler only warns: CS8425.

Inside the generator you pass the token further down, as in any async method (section 2).

cards.q: The generator's CancellationToken parameter has no attribute. The consumer writes .WithCancellation(cts.Token) and cancels. What happens?
options: The generator never sees the cancellation: the token went to GetAsyncEnumerator, and without [EnumeratorCancellation] it wasn't put into ct
The generator stops: WithCancellation passes the token to the first CancellationToken parameter
A compile error: without the attribute you can't call WithCancellation
cards.explain: ct stays default, a token that will never be canceled. The compiler warns about this (CS8425) but doesn't forbid it. Mark the parameter with the [EnumeratorCancellation] attribute.

wrong.1: WithCancellation doesn't touch the method's parameters: the token goes to GetAsyncEnumerator, and from there only into a parameter with the attribute.
wrong.2: It's warning CS8425, not an error: the code compiles and silently doesn't cancel.

cards.title: await using
cards.body:
If cleaning up a resource is itself asynchronous (flushing a buffer to the network, closing a connection), the type implements IAsyncDisposable with a ValueTask DisposeAsync() method. await using calls it at the end of the block and waits for it with await: the thread isn't blocked while the cleanup runs.

The compiler expands it into a try/finally with an await inside the finally, as in the comment below. You've already seen this mechanism: at the end, await foreach calls DisposeAsync on the enumerator.

A plain using would call the synchronous Dispose. For network resources it can block the thread while the remaining data is sent.

cards.q: How is await using different from using?
options: It calls DisposeAsync and waits for it with await, without blocking the thread
It isn't; they're synonyms
It frees the object's memory right away, without waiting for the GC
cards.explain: A plain using would call the synchronous Dispose, which can block the thread. In both cases the GC frees the object's memory: Dispose and DisposeAsync release resources, not memory.

cards.q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
options: await foreach iterates an IAsyncEnumerable
An async method with yield return declared as IAsyncEnumerable<T> is an async generator
The generator doesn't read the next item until the consumer asks for it
await using calls DisposeAsync
await foreach loads all the items at once
An async method with yield return can return Task<List<T>>
cards.explain: Items arrive one at a time, when the consumer asks. yield return in an async method is allowed only with IAsyncEnumerable<T> or IAsyncEnumerator<T>.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Run the generator to the next yield
The parameter that token lands in

lessons.title: Channel and Parallel.ForEachAsync
lessons.sub: Pipelines, completing a channel and limiting concurrency

cards.title: A channel is an async queue
cards.body:
Channel<T> is an asynchronous queue between parts of a program. A channel has two sides: Writer for producers and Reader for consumers. It's the async replacement for the "queue, lock and wait" combination: you wait on a channel with await, without blocking a thread.

Channel.CreateUnbounded<T>() accepts any number of items. Channel.CreateBounded<T>(100) holds at most 100. Here's what WriteAsync does on a bounded channel:

  • there's room: it adds the item and returns an already completed ValueTask, so the await goes through with no pause;
  • the channel already holds 100 items: it returns an unfinished ValueTask. The producer stops at the await, and the thread is free;
  • a consumer took an item: a slot frees up, the waiting writer's item goes into the channel, and its task completes.

This way a fast producer is forced to wait for a slow consumer. That's backpressure, like the generator's in the previous lesson. What happens when the channel is full is set in BoundedChannelOptions: the default is FullMode = Wait, and the DropOldest, DropNewest and DropWrite modes throw items away instead of waiting.

cards.q: A channel with room for 100 items is full, with default options. What does WriteAsync do?
options: Returns an unfinished task: the producer waits asynchronously until a slot frees up
Drops the oldest item
Throws an exception
cards.explain: That's the default behavior, FullMode = Wait. The channel drops items only if you explicitly pick DropOldest, DropNewest or DropWrite.

cards.title: End of the stream: Writer.Complete()
cards.body:
The channel doesn't know the producer is done: the producer's task completing tells it nothing. To a reader, an empty channel that isn't completed means "wait". The producer itself closes the channel: Writer.Complete() means "no more items". After that:

  • ReadAllAsync() returns an IAsyncEnumerable<T>: await foreach over it hands out what's left and exits once the channel is completed and empty. Inside it's a loop of WaitToReadAsync and TryRead, like the last snippet below;
  • WaitToReadAsync() waits until there's something to read and returns true, and on a completed empty channel returns false;
  • ReadAsync() returns the next item, and on a completed empty channel throws ChannelClosedException;
  • no more writing: WriteAsync throws ChannelClosedException, and TryWrite returns false.

Complete(ex) closes the channel with an error. Readers still get what's left, and then ReadAllAsync and WaitToReadAsync throw ex itself, while ReadAsync throws ChannelClosedException with ex as its InnerException. Forget Complete, and the consumers wait forever.

cards.q: The producer has finished. What does the consumer print?
options: 0…9, and "done" is never printed: the channel isn't completed, so await foreach waits for the next item
0…9 and "done": the producer finished, so there's no more data
0…9, then InvalidOperationException: there's nothing more to read
cards.explain: The channel doesn't know the producer is done: the producer's task finishing tells the channel nothing. To a reader, an empty channel that isn't completed means "wait". You need ch.Writer.Complete() after the loop, preferably in a finally.

cards.q: The producer wrote three items and called ch.Writer.Complete(new IOException("disk")). What does the consumer see?
options: It prints the three items, then await foreach throws IOException, and "done" is never printed
IOException right away: the items written before the error are lost
It prints the three items and "done": Complete closed the channel, and the loop ended as usual
cards.explain: Complete(ex) doesn't throw away what's left: the reader first gets everything that was written. On a completed empty channel ReadAllAsync (WaitToReadAsync inside it) throws the exception that was passed, so the producer's error reaches the consumer.

wrong.1: The channel hands out what's left even after Complete(ex): the error arrives only once the channel is empty.
wrong.2: That would happen with Complete() with no argument. Complete(ex) turns the end of the stream into an exception.

cards.title: Several consumers
cards.body:
There can be several consumers. Each item goes to exactly one of them: they share the stream of work rather than each getting a copy. It's a queue, not a broadcast: a taken item disappears from the channel, and the next one goes to whoever is free first.

Step by step for the code below. Four consumers start and stop at their await: the channel is empty. The producer writes while there's room, and every item taken frees a slot. After the last job the producer calls Complete, in a finally, so that the consumers exit even if it fails, and its own task carries the error. Each consumer, on seeing a completed empty channel, leaves its loop. WhenAll completes when all five are done.

cards.q: Two consumers read one channel through ReadAllAsync. The producer wrote 100 items and called Complete. How many does each get?
options: 100 between them: each item goes to exactly one, and how they split depends on their speed
100 each: both get a copy of every item
Exactly 50 each: the channel hands items out strictly in turn
cards.explain: A Channel is a queue: an item that's taken disappears from it. Whoever is free first takes the next one. If you need to send to everyone, give each recipient its own channel.

cards.title: Parallel.ForEachAsync
cards.body:
Since .NET 6 you can process a collection asynchronously with a concurrency limit. The mechanism: ForEachAsync starts up to N worker tasks. Each one takes the next item from a shared enumerator, calls the body, awaits it and takes the next item. So no more than N bodies run at once, and 10,000 requests won't go out all together.

  • N is set in ParallelOptions.MaxDegreeOfParallelism. If you don't set it, the default is Environment.ProcessorCount: there's always a limit.
  • The body gets a token ct. On the first exception ForEachAsync cancels that token, and the workers stop taking new items. When the bodies already started finish, the ForEachAsync task completes with an error, and await throws the body's exception.
  • Your own token goes into ParallelOptions.CancellationToken: ct in the body is canceled along with it.
cards.code:
await Parallel.ForEachAsync(urls,
    new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 8 },   // at most 8 bodies at once
    async (url, ct) => await DownloadAsync(url, ct));     // ct is canceled on the first error

cards.q: You need to download 10,000 files, at most 8 at a time. What do you pick?
options: Parallel.ForEachAsync with MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 8
Task.WhenAll on all 10,000 at once
A sequential await in a loop
cards.explain: WhenAll limits nothing by itself: all 10,000 requests go out at once and swamp the server. A sequential loop downloads one at a time and takes about 8 times longer. ForEachAsync keeps exactly 8 downloads running.

cards.q: Parallel.ForEachAsync is called without ParallelOptions on a machine with 16 logical cores. How many bodies run at once?
options: Up to 16: the default limit is Environment.ProcessorCount
All of them: without MaxDegreeOfParallelism there's no limit
One: without options the loop is sequential
cards.explain: ForEachAsync always has a limit. But for I/O the number of cores is an arbitrary figure: the API may handle more or fewer. So it's better to set the limit explicitly.

cards.title: The same by hand: SemaphoreSlim and WhenAll
cards.body:
You can build the same limit from the lock lesson: each download first takes a slot from a semaphore. new SemaphoreSlim(8) means 8 free slots and no upper limit. Step by step:

  • 1. Select calls the lambda for each url, and ToArray creates all 10,000 tasks right away.
  • 2. The first 8 get a slot: WaitAsync returned a completed task, and the download starts.
  • 3. The other 9,992 stop at await WaitAsync. They're just waiting tasks in the semaphore's queue; they hold no threads.
  • 4. A download finishes, and the Release in finally hands the slot to the next waiter.
  • 5. WhenAll completes when they're all done and returns an array of results in url order (section 2).

The difference from ForEachAsync: here all the tasks are created at once, 10,000 objects in memory, but WhenAll hands you an array of results. ForEachAsync keeps only N bodies running and takes items as it goes, and you collect the results yourself. A third way is a channel with N consumers, from the start of this lesson.

cards.q: The limit doesn't work: all 10,000 download at once. Which line is to blame?
cards.explain: WaitAsync without await is the same fire-and-forget from the first lesson. The ninth call gets an unfinished task, throws it away and goes straight to downloading. The compiler would have warned you: CS4014.

cards.q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
options: Each item in a channel goes to exactly one consumer
Without Writer.Complete(), await foreach over ReadAllAsync never ends
Parallel.ForEachAsync has a limit even if MaxDegreeOfParallelism isn't set
Task.WhenAll limits concurrency by itself
A Channel stores data on disk
cards.explain: WhenAll waits for whatever you give it; limiting is up to you: with a semaphore, ForEachAsync or a channel with N consumers. A Channel is an in-memory queue.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: A limit: the writer waits when there's no room
"No more is coming": readers leave the loop
Read until the channel is completed and empty
N worker tasks over one collection

lessons.title: Final: pitfalls
lessons.sub: Find the bug in each snippet

cards.q: Where is the bug?
cards.explain: InsertAsync without await: the inserts start all at once on one _db (that's a race), the commit runs before they finish, and their errors land in tasks nobody awaits.

cards.q: What won't compile?
cards.explain: CS1996: lock is a Monitor, and only the owner thread can release it, while after await another thread may continue the method. You need SemaphoreSlim: await WaitAsync before the try, Release in the finally.

cards.q: A TaskCompletionSource is completed from a library callback while the library holds its internal lock. What do you do so the waiters' code doesn't run under that lock?
options: Create it with TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously
Have the waiters write await tcs.Task.ConfigureAwait(false)
Nothing: continuations go to the pool anyway
cards.explain: With the flag, the waiters' continuations are queued, and SetResult immediately returns control to the library.

wrong.1: The opposite: with no context, the continuation is all the more certain to run right inside SetResult.
wrong.2: Without the flag and without a context, the continuation runs synchronously inside SetResult: on the library's thread, under its lock.

cards.q: A Channel pipeline: the producer wrote every item and returned, the consumers processed everything, but await Task.WhenAll(consumers) never completes. What's missing?
options: ch.Writer.Complete() in the producer
One more consumer
An unbounded channel instead of CreateBounded
cards.explain: To a reader, an empty channel that isn't completed means "wait for the next one". await foreach over ReadAllAsync exits only when the channel is completed and empty. Complete goes in the producer's finally.

cards.q: How can you limit the number of concurrent requests? Select all that apply.
options: Parallel.ForEachAsync with MaxDegreeOfParallelism
SemaphoreSlim(N, N) and await WaitAsync before each request
A bounded Channel and N consumers
Task.WhenAll on the whole collection
cards.explain: WhenAll limits nothing: it waits for whatever it's given. The other three keep no more than N requests running.

cards.q: _gate = new SemaphoreSlim(1, 1). SaveAsync, holding _gate, calls ValidateAsync, which also does await _gate.WaitAsync(). What happens?
options: It hangs forever: the semaphore has no owner, and ValidateAsync waits for the slot SaveAsync holds
It goes through: the call comes from the same chain, and the semaphore can see that
SynchronizationLockException: another method took the slot
cards.explain: A semaphore counts slots, not owners. Entering again is a silent deadlock: the Release in SaveAsync won't run until ValidateAsync completes, and ValidateAsync is waiting for that Release.

wrong.1: That's how the reentrant Monitor behaves. SemaphoreSlim doesn't know who took a slot.
wrong.2: SynchronizationLockException is what Monitor.Exit throws on a thread that isn't the owner. A semaphore has no owner, so there's nothing to check.

cards.q: Clean up the connection asynchronously
cards.code: ___ using var conn = new SqlConnection(cs);
cards.explain: await using calls DisposeAsync in a finally and waits for it without blocking the thread.

cards.q: Make the token from WithCancellation reach the generator
cards.explain: WithCancellation hands the token to GetAsyncEnumerator, and the generated enumerator puts it into the parameter marked [EnumeratorCancellation]. Without the attribute you get warning CS8425 and cancellation that silently doesn't work.

cards.q: A generator reads a huge file with await foreach and yield return, and the consumer spends a second on each line. How many lines does the generator read ahead?
options: None: it stays parked at yield return until the consumer asks for the next line
The whole file: the generator reads in the background while the consumer is busy
As many as fit in the IAsyncEnumerable's buffer
cards.explain: The generator runs only inside MoveNextAsync. While the consumer processes a line, the next MoveNextAsync hasn't been called, and the generator stays put. Memory holds one line, not the file (the file stream inside keeps only a small byte buffer).

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Complete a TaskCompletionSource task if it isn't complete yet
The token from WithCancellation has nowhere to go

units.title: Platforms
units.blurb: ASP.NET Core, WPF and WinForms, Unity: Awaitable, coroutines, UniTask and cancellation tied to the object.

lessons.title: ASP.NET Core
lessons.sub: No context, HttpContext lives until the request ends, work after the response goes to a BackgroundService

cards.title: What you already know: there is no context
cards.body:
From unit 4: in ASP.NET Core SynchronizationContext.Current == null. Any free pool thread runs the continuation after await, so the classic .Result deadlock doesn't happen. For the same reason ConfigureAwait(false) changes nothing in application code: there's nothing to capture and nowhere to return to. Libraries use it for callers that come from WPF or Unity.

But .Result hurts in Core too. While the database replies, the pool thread taken for the request just stands there doing nothing. Under load this produces an almost-deadlock, the pool starvation from u4.l5: every thread is stuck on .Result, and the continuations that would free them wait in the same pool queue behind new requests. Responses take seconds while the CPU sits idle.
cards.deep:
Why old ASP.NET hung. Old ASP.NET (.NET Framework) hung differently from WPF. It has no UI thread, but it does have a context: AspNetSynchronizationContext. It isn't a single thread but a rule: only one thread at a time runs inside a request's context. Step by step:

  • 1. The pool thread that took the request calls GetUserAsync; the await inside captures the request context.
  • 2. That thread blocks on .Result and keeps occupying the request context the whole time.
  • 3. The database replies. The continuation has to enter the request context, but a thread is already in there: the one blocked on .Result.
  • 4. Each waits for the other: a deadlock, even though a server has no "main" thread at all. This request and its thread hang; other requests are still served.

That's why libraries for old ASP.NET used ConfigureAwait(false): a continuation without a context doesn't need to enter the request, so the cycle never closes.

cards.task: An ASP.NET Core request handler calls .Result. The top lane is the thread running the handler: on a server it's also a pool thread taken for the request. Run it to the end: will it hang?
Rewrite the handler with await and run it to the end. Watch what the request thread does while the reply is on its way.

cards.q: ASP.NET Core on .NET 8, 8 cores. Every request does _repo.GetAsync(id).Result, and the database replies in 20 ms. 300 requests arrive at once: the CPU is at 5%, yet responses take 10-20 seconds. Why so long, if a deadlock is impossible in ASP.NET Core?
options: Threads are stuck on .Result, and the continuations that would free them wait in the pool queue behind new requests; the pool adds new threads with pauses
Without a SynchronizationContext a continuation runs only after the request has sent its response
Application code has no ConfigureAwait(false), so continuations wait for the request context
cards.explain: This is the almost-deadlock from u4.l5: the cycle breaks once the pool grows enough, but until then requests stand still. ConfigureAwait(false) is irrelevant: Core has no context. The cure is await all the way.

cards.title: HttpContext after await
cards.body:
After await, a controller method may be resumed by a different pool thread. That's fine for HttpContext: it's an ordinary object the controller references (the HttpContext property), not something tied to a thread. Until the request ends, HttpContext is available after any await, including after ConfigureAwait(false).

Old ASP.NET was different: the static HttpContext.Current was restored by AspNetSynchronizationContext, so after ConfigureAwait(false) it became null. Core has no HttpContext.Current.

cards.q: An ASP.NET Core controller. What happens on the HttpContext line?
options: It works: the request is still running, HttpContext is an ordinary object, and it doesn't matter which pool thread resumed the method
NullReferenceException: ConfigureAwait(false) lost the HttpContext
InvalidOperationException: HttpContext may only be touched from the thread that accepted the request
cards.explain: Thread affinity belonged to HttpContext.Current in old ASP.NET. In Core HttpContext is a controller property, and it's alive until the request ends.

cards.title: HttpContext: two rules and IHttpContextAccessor
cards.body:
The thread doesn't matter, but two rules remain:

  • 1. HttpContext isn't thread-safe. Sequential awaits are fine. Two parallel branches (WhenAll) that both read the request body or write headers are a race.
  • 2. HttpContext lives only until the request ends. After the response the server resets it and may hand the same object to the next request. A background task holding a reference reads someone else's data or empty fields, or gets ObjectDisposedException.

If a service needs HttpContext, it uses IHttpContextAccessor. It keeps a reference to a shared holder with the context in an AsyncLocal, so the value travels through await together with ExecutionContext (u3.l4). When the request ends, the server clears the holder itself, and accessor.HttpContext returns null, even in a task that inherited the ExecutionContext.

cards.q: AuditService (through IHttpContextAccessor) started a Task.Run from a request. The task reads accessor.HttpContext a minute later, long after the response went out. What does it get?
options: null: when the request ended, the server cleared the holder that every copy of the ExecutionContext shares
Its own request's HttpContext: the AsyncLocal was copied into the task along with the ExecutionContext
The HttpContext of whatever request the server is handling right now
cards.explain: The AsyncLocal did travel into the task, but what it holds isn't the HttpContext itself, it's a reference to a holder. When the request ends, the server clears the holder, and everyone referencing it sees null. Copy the data you need while the request is running.

wrong.1: The reference made it, but to a holder the server cleared when the request ended.
wrong.2: An AsyncLocal travels with the call chain, it doesn't live in a thread: another request's context won't show up in it.

cards.title: RequestAborted: the client left
cards.body:
The user closed the tab, and the server keeps running a heavy database query for a response nobody will receive. That's what the request's HttpContext.RequestAborted token is for: the server cancels it when the client drops the connection.

You don't need to type HttpContext.RequestAborted yourself. If a controller action or a minimal API handler has a CancellationToken parameter, ASP.NET Core passes exactly this token into it. From there it's u2.l5: pass it to every async call.

What happens on disconnect:

  • 1. The server cancels the token.
  • 2. The database driver or HttpClient that received the token aborts the operation and throws OperationCanceledException.
  • 3. The exception propagates up, no response is written: the client is gone. There's no need to treat it as an error.

Be careful with writes: if an operation must finish even without the client (the money is already charged, the order must be saved), don't give it RequestAborted.

cards.q: Abort the search if the client leaves
cards.explain: ASP.NET Core binds a CancellationToken parameter to HttpContext.RequestAborted. CancellationToken.None is never cancelled.

cards.title: Work after the response: your own scope and a queue
cards.body:
DI in ASP.NET Core creates scoped services once per request and disposes them when the request ends. The typical scoped service is EF Core's DbContext: it holds a database connection and isn't thread-safe.

What happens with _ = Task.Run(() => _db.SaveChangesAsync()) in a controller:

  • 1. Task.Run queues the lambda to the pool, and the controller returns Ok right away.
  • 2. The request ends, and DI disposes this request's DbContext.
  • 3. The lambda touches the disposed DbContext: ObjectDisposedException ("Cannot access a disposed context instance"). And if it started before the request finished its own database work, two operations run on one DbContext at once: a race.
  • 4. The exception sits in a task nobody awaits (u2.l3) and is lost.

The right way is to split the work. The request copies the data it needs into a queue and responds. A separate long-lived worker drains the queue and creates its own scope, with its own DbContext, for each item. The queue is a Channel from unit 5, the worker is a BackgroundService (next card).

cards.q: Which line is dangerous?
cards.explain: The scoped DbContext is disposed when the request ends, but the background task will still use it, or use it at the same time as the request. And nobody will see the error.

cards.title: BackgroundService and IHostedService from the inside
cards.body:
IHostedService is a two-method interface: the host calls StartAsync when the app starts and StopAsync when it stops. BackgroundService is a ready-made implementation for a long-running loop: you only write ExecuteAsync(stoppingToken).

  • 1. On startup, StartAsync calls ExecuteAsync, stores its task and doesn't wait for it: the app keeps starting.
  • 2. The loop in ExecuteAsync lives as long as the app runs.
  • 3. On shutdown, StopAsync cancels stoppingToken and waits for the ExecuteAsync task, but no longer than the host's shutdown timeout (HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout, 30 s by default).

A hosted service lives as a singleton, so it can't take a scoped service through its constructor: in Development DI reports an error right away, and without that check the DbContext would live forever and be shared across threads. You create the scope yourself with IServiceScopeFactory.CreateAsyncScope(), and await using (u5.l4) disposes it together with the DbContext.

Since .NET 6, an exception escaping ExecuteAsync stops the whole app by default (HostOptions.BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior = StopHost). So you catch a single item's error inside the loop and let OperationCanceledException through on shutdown.
cards.deep:
Up to and including .NET 9, the synchronous part of ExecuteAsync (everything before the first await that actually waits) ran right inside StartAsync, during host startup (recall u2.l1: until its first pause an async method is an ordinary method). Long synchronous code there delayed the start of the other services. In .NET 10 the whole of ExecuteAsync runs in the background.

The exception behavior is configurable: with the Ignore value, the host just logs the error instead of stopping. But then the failed loop silently stops working while the app looks alive.

cards.q: The try/catch around SendAsync was removed from EmailWorker. One day the SMTP server returned an error and SendAsync threw. What happens on .NET 8?
options: The exception completes the ExecuteAsync task, and the host stops the whole app
The exception is swallowed, and the loop moves on to the next email
The host restarts ExecuteAsync from the beginning
cards.explain: Since .NET 6 a failed BackgroundService stops the host by default. Catch a single email's error inside the loop.

lessons.title: WPF and WinForms
lessons.sub: Who checks the thread, how await returns via Post, Invoke, Progress<T> and Task.Run

cards.title: Who checks the thread: WPF
cards.body:
Why can't you touch a control from another thread? A Windows window belongs to the thread that created it: its messages arrive only in that thread's queue. And the internal structures of elements (the tree, layout, bindings) aren't protected by locks: they're designed for a single thread.

In WPF every element derives from DispatcherObject. On creation it remembers the current thread's Dispatcher, the object that manages that thread's queue. Reading and writing properties (Text, Content, Value...) starts with a VerifyAccess() check. Wrong thread: InvalidOperationException: The calling thread cannot access this object because a different thread owns it. The check always runs, in Debug and in Release. To check without an exception, call CheckAccess(): it returns false.

cards.q: A WPF button handler does await Task.Run(() => progressBar.Value = 50). What happens?
options: InvalidOperationException: the lambda runs on a pool thread, and the ProgressBar belongs to the UI thread
It works: Task.Run was called from the UI thread, so the lambda runs there
The exception only happens under a debugger; in Release the code works
cards.explain: Task.Run always hands the lambda to the pool. VerifyAccess in the Value setter sees a foreign thread and throws, in any WPF build. "Only under a debugger" is about WinForms.

cards.title: Who checks the thread: WinForms
cards.body:
In WinForms the check sits in access to the window handle (Control.Handle), which almost every property goes through: InvalidOperationException: Cross-thread operation not valid: Control 'label1' accessed from a thread other than the thread it was created on.

But it's switched on by the static Control.CheckForIllegalCrossThreadCalls flag, whose default value is Debugger.IsAttached: true only under a debugger. In a Release build without a debugger a cross-thread access may "work" and break the window later, at a random moment: a control doesn't repaint, the window hangs, an exception flies out somewhere else entirely. So no exception proves nothing. To find out whether you're on another thread, use InvokeRequired; more on it below.

cards.q: WinForms, a Release build running without a debugger. A System.Threading.Timer callback (it runs on a pool thread) writes label1.Text. What's most likely?
options: There may be no exception: the check is on by default only under a debugger, and the window may break later
Always InvalidOperationException "Cross-thread operation not valid"
A compile error: a control can't be accessed from a timer lambda
cards.explain: CheckForIllegalCrossThreadCalls defaults to true only when a debugger is attached. No exception doesn't mean the code is correct.

cards.title: How await gets back to the UI: Post and Send
cards.body:
From u4.l1: at the pause, await captures SynchronizationContext.Current and later calls its Post. A context has two main methods:

  • Post(callback): queue it to the target thread and return immediately;
  • Send(callback): run it on the target thread and wait until it finishes.

await only uses Post: the thread that completed the task has no reason to stand and wait for the UI thread.

In WPF the UI thread's context is DispatcherSynchronizationContext: its Post calls Dispatcher.BeginInvoke, and Send calls Dispatcher.Invoke. In WinForms it's WindowsFormsSynchronizationContext: Post calls Control.BeginInvoke, Send calls Control.Invoke. Both BeginInvokes do the same thing: put the delegate into the UI thread's queue, and the message loop runs it when it gets there.
cards.deep: DispatcherSynchronizationContext's Post queues the delegate at the Dispatcher's normal priority, which is higher than input and rendering. So a steady stream of short continuations (hundreds of Posts per second) can delay painting the window even though each piece is fast.

cards.task: After await the handler writes label.Text. Someone added ConfigureAwait(false), and everything broke. Fix it: the continuation must come back through Post into the UI thread's queue.

cards.title: Getting back to the UI thread by hand: Invoke and BeginInvoke
cards.body:
await brings you back to the UI on its own. But sometimes you're already on another thread with no await in sight: a System.Threading.Timer callback, a third-party library event. Then you call the Dispatcher or the control directly, the same calls that sit inside Post and Send:

  • Dispatcher.Invoke / Control.Invoke: run on the UI thread and wait until it's done;
  • Dispatcher.BeginInvoke / Control.BeginInvoke: queue it and return immediately;
  • Dispatcher.InvokeAsync: also queues it, but takes a plain lambda and returns an operation you can await (with a result, if the lambda returns one).

In WinForms InvokeRequired returns true when you're not on the UI thread. On .NET Framework a lambda for Control.Invoke and Control.BeginInvoke must be cast to a delegate explicitly (new Action(…)); newer WinForms versions on .NET have overloads that take an Action.

The Invoke trap is the same cycle as in u4.l2, just assembled by hand: 1) the UI thread is blocked on .Wait() of a background task; 2) the background calls Dispatcher.Invoke and waits for the UI thread; 3) the UI thread isn't draining its queue: deadlock. BeginInvoke and InvokeAsync don't wait, so they don't close that cycle.

cards.q: WPF. After a click the window hangs forever. Why?
options: Dispatcher.Invoke waits for the UI thread to run the delegate, but the UI thread is blocked on t.Wait() and isn't draining its queue
The Task.Run lambda runs on the UI thread, which is busy with t.Wait()
Dispatcher.Invoke can't be called from a pool thread: it throws, and the task never completes
cards.explain: The background waits for the UI thread, the UI thread waits for the background. With Dispatcher.InvokeAsync there'd be no cycle, but the window would still freeze on Wait(). The real fix is await t instead of t.Wait().

cards.title: Progress: Progress<T> and IProgress<T>
cards.body:
Background work often needs to report how it's going: "37%". You could call the Dispatcher straight from the computation, but then the computation knows about the window. The idiomatic way is the IProgress<T> interface with a single Report(T value) method, and its implementation Progress<T>:

  • 1. The Progress<T> constructor remembers SynchronizationContext.Current of the thread where it was created. Created in a handler, it remembers the UI thread's context.
  • 2. The background calls Report(i). Progress Posts to the remembered context and returns immediately: the computation doesn't wait for the UI.
  • 3. The UI thread takes the delegate from its queue and runs your callback: you can touch controls there.

Consequences. The callback arrives later than Report, so don't pass a mutable object: it may change before the callback runs. And if Progress is created where there's no context (inside Task.Run, in a console app), the callbacks go to the thread pool.

cards.q: WPF. Progress was created inside Task.Run. What happens when Import calls Report?
options: The callback runs on a pool thread and fails with InvalidOperationException on bar.Value
It works: Progress<T> always runs the callback on the UI thread
Report blocks the pool thread until the UI thread runs the callback
cards.explain: Progress remembers the context in its constructor, and on a pool thread SynchronizationContext.Current == null, so the callbacks go to the pool. Create Progress in the handler, before Task.Run.

cards.title: Where the window freezes: before await and after await
cards.body:
await by itself doesn't move work off the UI thread. The window freezes in two places:

  • 1. Before the first await. Until its first pause an async method works like an ordinary one (u2.l1): on the calling thread, that is, the UI thread.
  • 2. After await. The continuation came back to the UI thread through Post, and everything that follows runs there too. A heavy computation after awaiting a download freezes the window just as it would without any async.

The fix: hand the heavy part to the pool with Task.Run and show the result after await. If the method doesn't touch the UI itself (a computation in a library), you can put ConfigureAwait(false) on its await: then the pool runs the continuation along with the computation.

cards.q: WPF. After a click the window freezes for 3 seconds. Why?
options: HeavyCompute runs after await: the continuation came back to the UI thread
LoadAsync blocks the UI thread while it downloads
The await in Calc_Click holds the UI thread until CalculateAsync completes
cards.explain: await LoadAsync captured the DispatcherSynchronizationContext, and the HeavyCompute line ran on the UI thread. The fix: await Task.Run(() => HeavyCompute(data)), or ConfigureAwait(false) on await LoadAsync, since CalculateAsync doesn't touch the UI.

cards.q: The handler does await SaveReportAsync(), and the window freezes for 3 s right after the click. There's a ConfigureAwait(false), so why?
options: RenderPdf runs synchronously before the first await, on the UI thread; ConfigureAwait(false) only affects code after a pause
ConfigureAwait(false) sent the continuation back to the UI thread
File.WriteAllBytesAsync holds the UI thread until the write finishes
cards.explain: Before the first await the method is plain synchronous code on the calling thread. To leave the UI thread before the computation you need Task.Run: var pdf = await Task.Run(() => RenderPdf(report));

cards.q: A WPF handler: var mesh = await Task.Run(() => BuildMesh(points)); viewport.Show(mesh). Put what happens after the click in order
items: The handler starts on the UI thread
Task.Run queues the computation to the pool, await returns control
The UI thread is free and handles clicks
The computation finishes; Post sends the continuation into the UI thread's queue
The UI thread runs the code after await and shows the result
cards.explain: While the pool computes, the window stays alive: the UI thread drains the queue that the continuation will later arrive in.

lessons.title: Unity
lessons.sub: A queue drained once per frame, the main-thread check and Awaitable (Unity 2023.1+, Unity 6)

cards.title: UnitySynchronizationContext from the inside
cards.body:
At startup Unity installs a UnitySynchronizationContext on the main thread. It's simpler than the Dispatcher:

  • 1. Post adds the callback to a list under a lock. It can be called from any thread.
  • 2. Once per frame the player loop (the loop Unity runs every frame: input, Update, physics, rendering) takes the accumulated list on the main thread and runs everything in order.
  • 3. Anything added during that pass waits for the next frame.

So the continuation after awaiting a Task in a script runs on the main thread, but not immediately: at the next pass, up to a frame later.

And .Result on the main thread doesn't hang just the script, it hangs the whole game: the main thread is stuck, the frame never ends, the list is never drained, and the continuation .Result is waiting for never runs.

cards.title: Unity checks the thread, and whether the object is alive
cards.body:
Almost all of the Unity API (transform, GameObject, components, Instantiate) first checks that it was called from the main thread. Otherwise: UnityException: get_transform can only be called from the main thread (it starts with the name of the property or method you touched). From any thread you may only use what doesn't touch the engine: plain math (Vector3, Mathf) and your own C# objects.

Don't confuse it with MissingReferenceException. That one is about a destroyed object: the thread is right, but the object has already been destroyed (Destroy, a scene change). The C# reference is alive, but there's no engine object behind it: The object of type 'Transform' has been destroyed but you are still trying to access it. Why this happens with async is lesson 4.

cards.task: After an await with ConfigureAwait(false) the script moves the transform. Run it as is.

cards.q: Which error will Unity show?
options: UnityException: get_transform can only be called from the main thread
MissingReferenceException: The object of type 'Transform' has been destroyed
InvalidOperationException: The calling thread cannot access this object because a different thread owns it
cards.explain: ConfigureAwait(false) sent the continuation to the pool, and transform checked the thread. MissingReferenceException is about a destroyed object, and the InvalidOperationException with that text comes from WPF.

cards.task: Fix it: the continuation must return to the main thread through the UnitySynchronizationContext queue.
Unity can hang too. Drive it into a deadlock.

cards.q: Why does .Result in Start freeze the whole game and not just this script?
options: The main thread is stuck on .Result: the frame never ends, so there's no Update, no rendering and no draining of the context queue
Unity suspends every pool thread while a script waits for a task
UnitySynchronizationContext holds network replies until the end of the frame
cards.explain: The main thread drives the frame. While it's stuck, everything is stuck, including the queue where the continuation .Result needs is waiting.

cards.title: Awaitable: Unity's native async
cards.body:
Since Unity 2023.1 (and in Unity 6) an async method can return Awaitable instead of Task: a Unity class built for the game loop. Two main differences from Task:

  • 1. A continuation without a queue. In Unity, a Task brings its continuation back through UnitySynchronizationContext, up to a frame later. An Awaitable runs the continuation synchronously, at the moment the wait completes: Unity completes NextFrameAsync in the next frame and runs the code after await right then, without the context queue.
  • 2. Pooled instances. To avoid creating an object per wait, Unity takes Awaitables from a pool and returns them there after completion. That's why you may await one Awaitable only once: by the second await the instance may already belong to another operation. Unity calls this undefined behavior: sometimes an exception, sometimes a hang.

It's the same rule as for ValueTask (u3.l3), for the same reason: the object is reused. If several places need the result, keep the result itself or wrap the call in an async Task: a Task can be awaited any number of times.

cards.title: The Awaitable API map
cards.body:
Static Awaitable methods replace coroutine yield instructions and switch threads:

  • Awaitable.NextFrameAsync(): resume in the next frame;
  • Awaitable.EndOfFrameAsync(): at the end of the current frame, after rendering;
  • Awaitable.FixedUpdateAsync(): at the next physics step;
  • Awaitable.WaitForSecondsAsync(s): after s seconds;
  • Awaitable.FromAsyncOperation(op): when a Unity AsyncOperation finishes: loading a scene or an asset;
  • Awaitable.BackgroundThreadAsync(): resume on a pool thread;
  • Awaitable.MainThreadAsync(): return to the main thread (if already there, immediately, without a pause).

The frame, seconds and AsyncOperation waits also accept a CancellationToken (lesson 4). Between BackgroundThreadAsync and MainThreadAsync the code runs on the pool: you can't touch the Unity API there, or you get the same UnityException.

cards.q: Compute in the background, then move the object
cards.explain: Without MainThreadAsync the transform line runs on the pool and fails with UnityException.

cards.q: Unity 6. A script on the main thread does await Task.Delay(100) and then moves the transform. Where and when does the transform line run?
options: On the main thread, at the next pass over the UnitySynchronizationContext queue: up to a frame after Delay completed
On the timer thread, right after 100 ms, and it fails with UnityException
On the main thread, synchronously at the moment Delay completes, in the middle of the current Update
cards.explain: A Task brings its continuation back through Post into UnitySynchronizationContext, and the queue is drained once per frame. Resuming synchronously, without a queue, is what Awaitable does.

cards.q: Unity 6. What's wrong with this code?
options: A second await of the same Awaitable: the instance may be back in the pool and belong to another operation
Nothing: the second await returns the finished result right away, like with Task
A second await is only allowed after MainThreadAsync
cards.explain: One Awaitable, one await. If you need the result again, use the saved level or wrap the call in an async Task.

cards.q: Match them up
pairs: Wait for a scene or asset to load

lessons.title: Coroutines, UniTask and cancellation
lessons.sub: Who calls MoveNext, what stops a coroutine and an async method, destroyCancellationToken

cards.title: Coroutines from the inside
cards.body:
A coroutine is a method that returns IEnumerator and contains yield return. As with async (u3.l2), the compiler turns it into a state machine: each MoveNext call runs the code up to the next yield and stops.

  • 1. StartCoroutine(Blink()) runs the first MoveNext immediately and stores the enumerator under this MonoBehaviour.
  • 2. Whatever yield returned tells Unity when to call MoveNext again: null means the next frame, new WaitForSeconds(0.5f) means half a second later.
  • 3. MoveNext returned false: the coroutine is finished.
