Since Unity calls MoveNext itself, Unity decides when to stop. A coroutine stops when its object is destroyed, when the object is deactivated with gameObject.SetActive(false), and on StopCoroutine. But enabled = false on the script itself doesn't stop it: only Update and the script's other events are switched off.

Limitations. You can't return a value: yield hands instructions to Unity, not a result. yield return can't sit inside a try that has a catch (compile error CS1626). An exception in a coroutine is merely logged to the console by Unity and stops it; whoever started it never finds out.

cards.q: The Blink coroutine was started in Start. Then the script was switched off: enabled = false. What happens to the blinking?
options: It keeps going: disabling the component doesn't stop a coroutine
It stops, as with SetActive(false)
It pauses and resumes on enabled = true
cards.explain: A coroutine is stopped by destroying the object, SetActive(false) and StopCoroutine. enabled = false only switches off Update and the script's other events.

cards.title: async outlives the object
cards.body:
For an async method, MoveNext is called by the waiting machinery: an Awaitable, a task through the UnitySynchronizationContext queue, a pool thread. None of them knows which GameObject the method belongs to. So destroying the object doesn't stop an async method. Step by step (numbers match the code):

  • 1. While the method waits for 5 seconds, the object is destroyed: Destroy, a scene change.
  • 2. The wait knows nothing about the object: it completes and calls MoveNext.
  • 3. Unity overrides == for its objects: a destroyed object "equals null" even though the C# reference is alive.
  • 4. Touching the engine side (transform, components) throws MissingReferenceException. The script's ordinary C# fields can still be read.

The editor has one more case: you exit Play Mode, the scene is unloaded, and running Tasks keep working until they finish.

cards.q: The object is destroyed during await Awaitable.WaitForSecondsAsync(5). What happens to an async method without a cancellation token?
options: It keeps running and fails with MissingReferenceException on the first access to transform
It stops, like a coroutine
Unity cancels it automatically when the object is destroyed
cards.explain: An async method's MoveNext is called by the completed wait, not by Unity. You have to stop it explicitly, with a cancellation token.

cards.title: destroyCancellationToken
cards.body:
Since Unity 2022.2 every MonoBehaviour has a destroyCancellationToken: Unity cancels it when this MonoBehaviour is destroyed (Destroy, a scene unload). Pass it into your waits:

  • 1. The object is destroyed during WaitForSecondsAsync(2f, ct).
  • 2. The token is cancelled: the wait is aborted, and await throws OperationCanceledException (u2.l5).
  • 3. The lines after await don't run: the exception propagates up. Without a catch the method would end in the Canceled state; in the code below a catch swallows it, because cancellation isn't an error.
  • 4. Cleanup goes in finally: it runs on cancellation too. Just don't touch this object's Unity API there: the object is gone.

The token is cancelled only on destruction: SetActive(false) and enabled = false leave it alone, so a deactivated object keeps patrolling. And it only works where you passed it: an await without the token won't notice the cancellation. Grab the token into a variable at the start of the method, while the object is alive: on an already destroyed object, merely reading destroyCancellationToken throws.

cards.q: Stop the patrol together with the object
cards.code: await Awaitable.WaitForSecondsAsync(2f, ___);
cards.explain: CancellationToken.None is never cancelled, and gameObject and this aren't tokens.

cards.q: Unity 6. PatrolAsync is running with destroyCancellationToken. The object is deactivated: gameObject.SetActive(false). What happens?
options: The patrol continues: the token is cancelled only when the object is destroyed
The patrol stops, just as a coroutine would
await throws OperationCanceledException, and on SetActive(true) the patrol resumes where it left off
cards.explain: SetActive(false) stops coroutines, but it doesn't cancel destroyCancellationToken. If you need to stop on deactivation, pass your own token and call Cancel on its CancellationTokenSource in the same place where you deactivate the object.

cards.title: UniTask
cards.body:
UniTask is a free library by Cysharp (installed as a package from GitHub or OpenUPM). It appeared long before Awaitable, and here's how it works:

  • UniTask and UniTask<T> are structs, like ValueTask (u3.l3): almost no allocations, and the same rule: one UniTask is awaited once. Need more: .Preserve().
  • UniTask continuations don't go through a SynchronizationContext: the library plugs its own points into Unity's player loop and resumes wherever you asked: UniTask.Yield(PlayerLoopTiming.Update), UniTask.NextFrame(), UniTask.Delay(ms).
  • Wrappers for Unity's asynchronous API (AsyncOperation, UnityWebRequest, uGUI events) with cancellation via .WithCancellation(ct).
  • It has UniTask.WhenAll and UniTask.WhenAny; Awaitable has no combinators of its own.

When to use which: in Unity 6 the built-in Awaitable is enough for simple code. UniTask is chosen for its rich API and combinators, and in projects on Unity before 2023.1 because Awaitable doesn't exist there.

cards.title: Coroutine, Awaitable, UniTask: what stops what
cards.body:
The same patrol written three ways (code below), and who stops it:

  • Destroy: a coroutine stops on its own; Awaitable and UniTask only if destroyCancellationToken was passed into the waits.
  • SetActive(false): a coroutine stops; Awaitable and UniTask don't, even with destroyCancellationToken.
  • enabled = false: stops none of them.
  • Returning a result: a coroutine can't; Awaitable<T> and UniTask<T> can.
  • An exception: a coroutine only logs it to the console; async puts it into the task, for whoever awaits it (u2.l3).

Unity stops a coroutine because it calls the coroutine's MoveNext itself. Only a token stops async methods, because their MoveNext is called by the completed wait.

cards.q: Unity 6. You need to download JSON from a server, return the parsed object to the game, and not crash if the window with this script was closed (the object destroyed). What fits?
options: async Awaitable<T> or UniTask<T>, with destroyCancellationToken passed into the waits
Task.Run(() => Load()).Result in Start
An async void method without a token that writes the result into a field
cards.explain: The result and exceptions come through await, cancellation on destruction comes from the token. .Result would freeze the main thread, and async void without a token keeps running after destruction and fails when it touches the object.

cards.q: Match each tool to what it is
pairs: A library: a struct, continuations in the player loop
Cancelled when the object is destroyed

cards.q: What's true? Select all that apply.
options: A coroutine stops when its MonoBehaviour is destroyed
An async method stops on its own when the object is destroyed
destroyCancellationToken is cancelled when the object is destroyed
enabled = false stops the script's coroutines
One UniTask, like one Awaitable, is awaited only once
cards.explain: async has to be cancelled with a token, and enabled = false doesn't stop a coroutine: it only switches off Update and the script's events.

lessons.title: Final: platforms
lessons.sub: Server, window and game: one mechanism

cards.task: Find the environment where .Result doesn't hang.
A Unity script moves the transform after await. Make it work without freezing frames.

cards.q: What do WPF and Unity have in common for async?
options: Both install a SynchronizationContext on the main thread whose Post puts the continuation into that thread's queue
Both run every continuation on a pool thread, and the main thread only renders
Both forbid .Result at the compiler level
cards.explain: That's why .Result on the main thread hangs in both: the queue has to be drained by the very thread that's stuck on .Result.

cards.q: Where is ConfigureAwait(false) dangerous? Select all that apply.
options: In a WPF handler that then changes a control
In a Unity script that then touches the transform
In an HTTP client library
In an ASP.NET Core controller
cards.explain: After it the code runs on the pool: VerifyAccess in WPF and Unity's main-thread check will throw. In a library it helps, and in ASP.NET Core there's no context, so it changes nothing.

cards.q: Which line is missing cancellation?
cards.explain: Without destroyCancellationToken the wait isn't cancelled if the object is destroyed, and the next line fails with MissingReferenceException.

cards.q: After a payment, an ASP.NET Core controller does _ = Task.Run(() => _mailer.SendReceiptAsync(order.Id)); _mailer is a scoped service with a DbContext inside. What's the right way?
options: Put order.Id into a Channel queue, and a BackgroundService sends the email in its own scope
Add ConfigureAwait(false) to SendReceiptAsync inside Task.Run
Call SendReceiptAsync from an async void method so the error isn't lost
cards.explain: The scoped DbContext is disposed together with the request. Work after the response belongs in a BackgroundService that creates its own scope for each queue item.

cards.q: Put the continuation's path after await in WPF in order
items: await captured the DispatcherSynchronizationContext
The operation completed on a pool thread
Post calls Dispatcher.BeginInvoke: the continuation is queued to the UI thread
The UI thread took it from the queue
The code after await ran on the UI thread
cards.explain: If the UI thread is blocked on .Result at that moment, step 4 never comes: that's the deadlock.

cards.q: WPF: a Progress<int> is created in a button handler, and Report is called from Task.Run. Where does the Progress callback run?
options: On the UI thread: Progress remembered the DispatcherSynchronizationContext and Posts to it
On the pool thread that called Report
Synchronously inside Report: the pool thread waits for the callback to run
cards.explain: Progress remembers the context in its constructor. Report only queues the callback and returns immediately.

cards.q: Unity 6. An object runs the Blink coroutine and an async Awaitable PatrolAsync with destroyCancellationToken at the same time. The object is deactivated: SetActive(false). What stops?
options: Only the coroutine
Both: SetActive(false) also cancels destroyCancellationToken
Nothing: SetActive(false) stops neither
cards.explain: Unity stops the coroutine because it calls the coroutine's MoveNext itself. destroyCancellationToken is cancelled only when the object is destroyed.

cards.q: Match each platform to how await brings the continuation back
pairs: A queue drained once per frame
No context: the continuation runs on the pool

cards.q: Which rule saves the server, the window and the game alike?
options: Async all the way: don't block async code with .Result and .Wait()
Put Task.Run everywhere
Always use ConfigureAwait(false)
cards.explain: Blocking the main thread in WPF and Unity gives a deadlock, on a server it gives pool starvation. Task.Run and ConfigureAwait(false) are tools for specific places, not a general rule.

units.title: Tasks without await
units.blurb: ContinueWith and its traps, TaskScheduler and StartNew vs. Task.Run, child tasks, Parallel and PLINQ for CPU work, timers and who holds them, background threads, Register and linked tokens.

lessons.title: ContinueWith and its traps
lessons.sub: Continuations by hand: scheduler, exceptions, options, token and Unwrap

cards.title: A continuation by hand
cards.body:
Before await there was ContinueWith (.NET 4.0). It hangs a delegate on a task: when the antecedent task finishes — in any way: success, failure or cancellation — the delegate is queued to a scheduler.

ContinueWith itself immediately returns a new task — the continuation task. It completes once the delegate has run.
cards.deep:
A task has a field for continuations (m_continuationObject): it holds one object or a list. When the task completes, it walks that field. For ContinueWith the entry is a wrapper that queues a new Task to the scheduler.

await uses the same field but puts the state machine box there (unit 3, "Under the hood"). Hence the cost difference: each ContinueWith is a new task and a delegate (plus a closure), while an async method gets by with one box for the whole method.

cards.q: load completed with an error. What happens to the continuation load.ContinueWith(t => Log("done"))?
options: It runs: without options a continuation runs on any outcome
It does not run: the antecedent failure cancels the continuation
It throws AggregateException on the thread that called ContinueWith
It runs, but only after an explicit load.Wait()
cards.explain: By default (TaskContinuationOptions.None) a continuation does not care how the antecedent ended. Dealing with the error is its own job.

wrong.1: Only a continuation told by an option to run on success alone behaves like that — options come later in this lesson.

cards.title: Trap 1: TaskScheduler.Current
cards.body:
A continuation is run by a task scheduler (TaskScheduler; more in the next lesson). ContinueWith without an explicit scheduler takes TaskScheduler.Current — the scheduler of the task whose code is running right now on this thread. Outside any task that is TaskScheduler.Default, i.e. the thread pool.

A scheduler for the UI thread comes from TaskScheduler.FromCurrentSynchronizationContext(). At the moment of the call it captures SynchronizationContext.Current and hands every task to it via Post — the same path into the UI thread's queue that await uses (unit 6). You call it on the UI thread: where there is no context, it throws InvalidOperationException.

The trap: a task on the UI scheduler itself becomes the "current" one. Inside it Current is the UI scheduler, and any "background" continuation without a scheduler silently moves to the UI thread. The window freezes even though no UI appears anywhere in the code.

Task.Factory.StartNew follows the same logic. Its full overload takes four arguments: the delegate, a token, creation options (TaskCreationOptions, next lesson) and a scheduler; without a scheduler it also takes Current. The rule: always pass the scheduler explicitly to ContinueWith and StartNew. Analyzer CA2008 warns you if you forget.
cards.deep:
await works differently: it first looks at SynchronizationContext.Current, and only when there is no context does it look at TaskScheduler.Current, and only if that is not Default. That is why after await in UI code you come back to the UI thread through the context, not through a scheduler.

The TaskCreationOptions.HideScheduler option hides the scheduler: inside such a task Current looks like Default, and nested code does not inherit the UI scheduler.

cards.q: This code runs on the WPF UI thread. Which thread runs Heavy()?
options: The UI thread
A thread-pool thread
A new dedicated thread
The pool, if it has a free thread
cards.explain: The inner StartNew without a scheduler takes TaskScheduler.Current. The outer task runs on the UI scheduler, so Current is that scheduler, and Heavy() goes to the UI thread too. The fix is TaskScheduler.Default or Task.Run.

cards.title: Trap 2: exceptions
cards.body:
A continuation receives the antecedent as is. If it failed, t.Result throws AggregateException — like .Result in unit 2, only now inside the continuation.

That exception faults the continuation task. And usually nobody waits for it: the result of ContinueWith was thrown away. The outcome is silence: no error dialog, no log line. With await the exception would have reached the caller.

So check the outcome yourself in a continuation: t.IsFaulted, t.IsCanceled, t.Exception.
cards.deep:
What happens to an unobserved error: when the garbage collector collects a faulted task whose exception nobody read, the runtime raises TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException.

Then and now: in .NET 4.0 the process crashed after that. Since .NET 4.5 nothing happens by default (the ThrowUnobservedTaskExceptions setting could bring the crash back). In .NET Core and .NET 5+ there is only the event. So a lost error does not crash the app — it just vanishes, which is worse for debugging.

cards.q: LoadAsync failed. On which line is the exception thrown and lost without a trace?
cards.explain: t.Result on a faulted task throws AggregateException. It faults the continuation task, and nobody waits for it: Refresh did not even keep it. Render is never called, and nobody finds out.

cards.title: Outcome options and Canceled
cards.body:
TaskContinuationOptions flags say on which outcome of the antecedent the continuation should run. There are six:

  • OnlyOnRanToCompletion, OnlyOnFaulted, OnlyOnCanceled — only on that outcome;
  • NotOnRanToCompletion, NotOnFaulted, NotOnCanceled — on any outcome except that one.

The trap: if the condition is not met, the delegate does not run, and the continuation task moves to Canceled. Wait for it and you get TaskCanceledException.

And that cancellation spreads. Task.WhenAll (unit 2) looks at the outcomes of all its tasks: 1) one has failed — it is Faulted itself, with all the exceptions; 2) none failed but one was cancelled — it is Canceled itself, and await on it throws TaskCanceledException; 3) otherwise — success.
cards.deep: OnlyOnRanToCompletion is just NotOnFaulted | NotOnCanceled, and OnlyOnFaulted is NotOnRanToCompletion | NotOnCanceled. The "Not" flags add up, and the runtime rejects all three together with ArgumentOutOfRangeException: such a continuation could never run.

cards.q: In the code above load completed successfully. What happens at await err?
options: TaskCanceledException
Completes instantly without an error
Waits forever
NullReferenceException from t.Exception!
cards.explain: The OnlyOnFaulted condition was not met, the delegate never ran, and err moved to Canceled. Awaiting a cancelled task throws TaskCanceledException.

wrong.2: err does not hang: it was moved to Canceled right away.
wrong.3: The delegate never ran — it never got to t.Exception.

cards.title: A task inside a task: Unwrap
cards.body:
If the continuation is itself asynchronous and returns a Task, ContinueWith returns Task<Task>. The outer task completes as soon as the lambda has returned the inner one — that is, at the first real await inside. You will not wait for the end of the work that way.

Unwrap() builds a proxy task: it completes together with the inner task — with its result, error or cancellation. Task.Factory.StartNew with an async lambda has the same story — we will take it apart in the next lesson.
cards.deep:
Unwrap is an extension method from TaskExtensions, available for Task<Task> and Task<Task<T>>. It blocks nothing: the proxy subscribes to the outer task, then to the inner one. If the outer task failed or was cancelled, the proxy takes that outcome.

Task.Run with a Func<Task> does this unwrapping internally. await await nested also works, but reads worse.

cards.q: Run SaveAsync after load on the pool and get a task that completes together with the save
cards.explain: Default is the pool, no matter who called the code. Unwrap turns Task<Task> into a task that waits for the save itself, not just for its start.

cards.title: How to run and when to cancel
cards.body:
Two more options are about how to run a continuation:

  • ExecuteSynchronously — run right on the thread that completed the antecedent, without the scheduler's queue. Only for short continuations: a long one holds up that thread and everything waiting behind it;
  • RunContinuationsAsynchronously — do not run the continuations of the continuation itself synchronously, as with TaskCompletionSource in unit 5.

ContinueWith has overloads with a token: ContinueWith(action, ct) and the full ContinueWith(action, ct, options, scheduler). Step by step, without options: 1) the antecedent is still running; 2) the token is cancelled — the continuation moves to Canceled at once, and the delegate will never run; 3) whoever waits for the continuation moves on, although the antecedent has not finished and may still be writing to the same data.

The LazyCancellation option changes step 2: the continuation becomes Canceled only after the antecedent completes. The chain does not overtake itself.
cards.deep: ExecuteSynchronously is a request, not an order. If the antecedent has already completed when ContinueWith is called, the continuation runs right on the calling thread. A long chain of such continuations could dive deep into the stack, so the runtime watches the remaining stack and queues the continuation anyway when an overflow threatens. The scheduler may also refuse inlining.

cards.q: What happens at await cont, and when?
options: TaskCanceledException almost at once, while load is still running
TaskCanceledException after 3 s, when load finishes
Prints cont after 3 s: cancellation is checked only before the antecedent starts
Prints cont almost at once: Cancel runs the continuation early
cards.explain: Without LazyCancellation the continuation becomes Canceled the moment the token is cancelled, without waiting for the antecedent. The delegate will not run, and await cont throws TaskCanceledException while load is still sleeping.

wrong.1: That is what LazyCancellation would do: it postpones the cancellation until the antecedent ends.

cards.title: When ContinueWith still fits
cards.body:
await does all of that and more: it returns to the context, unwraps the exception and does not create a task per step. So await is the default.

ContinueWith remains for narrow cases:

  • hanging a cheap handler without making the method async — for example, logging the error of a task nobody awaits;
  • hot library code: the overload with state and a static lambda avoid a closure;
  • old code from the .NET 4.0 days.

The example below brings the whole lesson together: an outcome option, a short continuation without a queue, the pool chosen explicitly, and state instead of a closure.
cards.code:
static void LogIfFaulted(this Task task, ILogger log) =>
    task.ContinueWith(static (t, s) =>
            ((ILogger)s!).LogError(t.Exception, "Background task failed"),
        log, CancellationToken.None,
        TaskContinuationOptions.OnlyOnFaulted |
        TaskContinuationOptions.ExecuteSynchronously,
        TaskScheduler.Default);

cards.q: What is true about ContinueWith? Select all.
options: Without options a continuation runs on any outcome of the antecedent
Without an explicit scheduler it takes TaskScheduler.Current
An exception in the continuation reaches whoever called ContinueWith
A continuation with OnlyOnFaulted moves to Canceled after a success
Without LazyCancellation, cancelling the token makes the continuation Canceled without waiting for the antecedent
Unwrap blocks the thread until the inner task ends
cards.explain: A continuation's exception stays in the continuation task — only whoever waits for it will see it. Unwrap blocks nothing; it builds a proxy task.

lessons.title: The scheduler and StartNew
lessons.sub: TaskScheduler, the pool's queues, TaskCreationOptions and child tasks

cards.title: Who runs a task: TaskScheduler
cards.body:
A task that has a delegate does not start itself. It is handed to a task scheduler (TaskScheduler), which decides where and when to run it:

  • TaskScheduler.Default — the thread pool;
  • FromCurrentSynchronizationContext() — into the current context, for example the UI thread (last lesson);
  • ConcurrentExclusiveSchedulerPair — a ready-made pair for limits: "no more than N at once" and "strictly one at a time".

Tasks from async methods and TaskCompletionSource have no delegate: they are not run but completed from outside — by the state machine builder (unit 3) or by your code via SetResult (unit 5). They need no scheduler.
cards.deep:
A custom scheduler derives from TaskScheduler and implements three methods: QueueTask (accept a task), TryExecuteTaskInline (may it run right now on this thread) and GetScheduledTasks (for the debugger).

Inlining happens, for example, on Wait() for a task that has not started yet: the waiting thread may run it itself instead of standing idle. One more detail: if there is no SynchronizationContext and TaskScheduler.Current is not Default, await resumes on that scheduler. Code under a ConcurrentExclusiveSchedulerPair stays under it after await.

cards.q: Which task never goes through a TaskScheduler at all?
options: A task returned by an async method
A task from Task.Run
A task from Task.Factory.StartNew
A continuation task from ContinueWith
cards.explain: An async method's task is a promise without a delegate: the state machine builder completes it. The other three carry a delegate, and someone has to run it — that is exactly the scheduler's job.

cards.title: Task.Run is StartNew with the right settings
cards.body:
Task.Run arrived in .NET 4.5 as a shorthand for the most common case. It equals StartNew with three explicit decisions: no token, no child attachment (DenyChildAttach, covered at the end of the lesson), strictly the pool. And for an async lambda it also does Unwrap.

A "bare" Task.Factory.StartNew(work) differs in everything: scheduler Current (the trap from the last lesson), options None, no unwrapping. With an async lambda it returns Task<Task>, and the outer task completes at the first real await inside.

You need StartNew when you need what it offers: a custom scheduler, LongRunning, a state object without a closure.

cards.q: What does this code print?
options: About 0
About 1000
About 2000
Does not compile: StartNew does not accept an async lambda
cards.explain: StartNew returned Task<Task>. The outer task completed when the lambda reached its first await and returned the inner task. await waited only for that. With Task.Run it would be about 1000.

cards.title: Inside the pool: the global and local queues
cards.body:
TaskScheduler.Default hands tasks to the thread pool. The pool has more than one queue:

  • the global queue — shared, FIFO. Work queued from outside the pool lands there: from Main, from the UI thread, from your own Thread. The timer service thread also queues timer callbacks there;
  • a local queue — one per pool worker thread. A task created inside a pool thread (Task.Run or StartNew from another task) goes to that thread's local queue.

Once free, a pool thread looks for work in this order:

  • 1. Its own local queue, from the end: the most recently added task first (LIFO). Its data is most likely still in the CPU cache.
  • 2. The global queue.
  • 3. Other threads' local queues, from the front — the oldest tasks. This is work stealing: an idle thread takes tasks away from a busy one.

Local queues remove the crowding around a single shared queue, but the order stops being fair: a thread that spawns subtasks runs them before requests that have long been waiting in the global queue. The PreferFairness option (next card) puts a task into the global queue even from a pool thread. How many threads the pool has and how quickly it adds new ones (MinThreads, SetMinThreads) was covered in unit 4.
cards.deep:
A local queue is a special structure (WorkStealingQueue in the sources): the owner pushes and pops at one end almost without synchronization, while thieves take from the other end under a lock. So the expensive synchronization is paid only on a steal, not on every task.

ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem(cb) goes to the global queue by default even from a pool thread; the local queue is chosen with the preferLocal: true overload. When there is a lot of work and few threads, the pool may add a thread, and that thread starts by stealing.

cards.q: A task on pool thread P calls Task.Run(Step1), Task.Run(Step2), Task.Run(Step3) in turn and finishes. The pool's other threads are busy. Which step does P take first?
options: Step3: a thread works through its local queue from the end
Step1: the pool's queues are strictly FIFO
None of them: Task.Run always uses the global queue, and the steps wait behind everything
None of them: a thread does not touch its own queue; the steps wait until another thread steals them
cards.explain: The steps were created inside a pool thread and went to its local queue. The owner takes from the end — Step3, then Step2 and Step1. If another thread freed up, it would steal from the front — Step1. If you need an order, do not rely on the pool's queues: await the steps one by one or pass the work through a channel.

wrong.1: Only the global queue and stealing from the front of another queue are FIFO. The owner takes from its own queue at the end.
wrong.2: Task.Run uses the global queue only when called from outside the pool or with PreferFairness.

cards.title: TaskCreationOptions
cards.body:
Creation options are hints for the scheduler and rules for task relationships:

  • LongRunning — work that takes a long time. The default scheduler gives it a dedicated thread instead of a pool thread: the pool keeps its worker and does not have to wait to inject new threads. It is only a hint: a custom scheduler may ignore it. And the thread serves a single delegate: with an async lambda the delegate returns at the first real pause, the thread exits, and the continuations after await already run on the pool;
  • PreferFairness — put the task into the global queue rather than the local one, even from a pool thread: closer to first come, first served. It does not make the task any faster;
  • AttachedToParent and DenyChildAttach — task relationships, more on them below;
  • HideScheduler — inside the task TaskScheduler.Current looks like Default;
  • RunContinuationsAsynchronously — as with TaskCompletionSource in unit 5.
cards.deep: In the default scheduler LongRunning is literal: it creates new Thread(…) { IsBackground = true }, which runs one task and exits. Creating a thread means an OS object and a stack reservation, on the order of tens of microseconds or more. For short tasks the option hurts.

cards.q: How long does the dedicated thread allocated for LongRunning live?
options: Until the first real pause at an await
As long as the loop spins, i.e. forever
Not at all: the option fails with an async lambda
Until the garbage collector collects the task
cards.explain: The delegate is an async lambda. At the first incomplete await it returns a task, and the thread is free — so it exits. The loop continues on pool threads. The dedicated thread was created for nothing. This loop does not need LongRunning: it does not hold a thread anyway.

cards.title: Child tasks and DenyChildAttach
cards.body:
A task created inside a running task with AttachedToParent becomes its child:

  • the parent does not complete until all its children have. While it waits, its status is WaitingForChildrenToComplete;
  • children's exceptions end up in the parent's AggregateException.

Without the option a nested task is independent (detached): the parent knows nothing about it. This is the "structured parallelism" model of .NET 4.0. New code does the same explicitly: collect the tasks and wait with WhenAll.

Whether to attach is decided by the child, that is, by someone else's code. If a library creates a child with AttachedToParent inside your task, your task suddenly waits for foreign work and receives foreign exceptions. DenyChildAttach on the parent silently cancels such requests: the child becomes an ordinary independent task, without any error. Task.Run always sets it.
cards.deep: How it works: on creation a task checks which task is currently running on this thread. If AttachedToParent is set and that task has no DenyChildAttach, the parent's counter of unfinished children goes up. When the parent finishes its delegate, it decrements the counter for itself; each child decrements it on completion. Zero means the parent is complete.

cards.q: What does the code print?
options: parent, child, done
parent, done, child
child, parent, done
done, parent, child
cards.explain: The child is attached: Wait on the parent waits for it too. "parent" prints at once, "child" after 500 ms, and only then is the parent complete and "done" printed.

cards.q: The same code, but the outer StartNew is replaced with Task.Run, and the program waits for Enter at the end. What is printed?
options: parent, done, child: the child did not attach
parent, child, done: the child's option beats the parent's settings
parent and InvalidOperationException: attaching is forbidden
parent, done — and nothing more: Task.Run cancels the unattached child
cards.explain: Task.Run sets DenyChildAttach, and the child's AttachedToParent is silently ignored. Wait covers only the parent body: "parent", "done", and "child" after 500 ms. The process is still alive thanks to ReadLine, so the child gets to print.

cards.q: Hardware polling is a blocking loop that runs for hours. Give it a dedicated thread without touching the pool, strictly through the standard scheduler
cards.code:
Task.Factory.StartNew(PollHardware,
    CancellationToken.None,
    TaskCreationOptions.___ | TaskCreationOptions.DenyChildAttach,
    TaskScheduler.___);
cards.explain: LongRunning with the default scheduler gives a dedicated thread. Default so as not to depend on which task the code is called from.

cards.q: What is true? Select all.
options: Task.Run always uses TaskScheduler.Default
Task.Factory.StartNew without a scheduler takes TaskScheduler.Current
Task.Run unwraps the Task<Task> from an async lambda
A task created on a pool thread goes to that thread's local queue by default
LongRunning guarantees a dedicated thread with any scheduler
PreferFairness makes a task run faster
cards.explain: LongRunning is a hint: only the default scheduler turns it into a dedicated thread. PreferFairness changes the queue, not the speed.

cards.q: Match the option to its effect
pairs: A dedicated thread instead of the pool
The global queue instead of the local one
The parent waits for this child

lessons.title: Parallel and PLINQ
lessons.sub: Every core on one job — and when it does not pay off

cards.title: Data parallelism
cards.body:
async is about waiting. This is something else: computation. The same operation over many elements, spread across all cores. For that there are Parallel.For, Parallel.ForEach, Parallel.Invoke and PLINQ.

The key fact about Parallel.For: it is synchronous. The calling thread blocks until all iterations finish, and it takes iterations itself too. Pool threads pick up the rest.

This is a tool for CPU work. For I/O there is Parallel.ForEachAsync from unit 5; how the two differ is covered later in this lesson.
cards.deep:
Inside, Parallel creates a "replicating" task: the calling thread runs it itself, and its copies go to the pool. Each copy grabs ranges of indices, and the ranges grow as work proceeds — this balances the load even when iterations differ in length.

If the loop body blocks, the pool injects threads, and the loop happily takes those too: by default it has no limit. So a blocking body in Parallel is a road to the pool starvation from unit 4.

cards.q: A WPF button handler calls Parallel.For with 3 seconds of heavy work. What happens to the window?
options: It freezes: Parallel.For is synchronous and occupies the calling thread
It does not freeze: all iterations go to the pool
It throws InvalidOperationException: not allowed from the UI thread
It freezes only on a single-core machine
cards.explain: The UI thread waits for the loop to end and computes iterations itself. The fix: await Task.Run(() => Parallel.For(…)) — then a pool thread does the waiting and the UI thread is free.

cards.title: Shared data: races and local totals
cards.body:
Iterations run at the same time. Each writing its own cell is fine. Changing a shared variable is a race. count++ looks like one operation, but the CPU does three steps: read the value from memory, add 1, write it back. Step by step, two threads, count = 5:

  • 1. Thread A read 5.
  • 2. Thread B read 5 — A has not written yet.
  • 3. A wrote 6.
  • 4. B wrote 6. There were two increments, but the counter went up by one.

There are two cures. Interlocked.Increment(ref x) and Interlocked.Add(ref x, n) do the read-add-write as one atomic CPU instruction: nobody can squeeze in between the read and the write. That is cheaper than a lock, but not free under contention either (how it works — unit 8). A lock in every iteration, on the other hand, lines the threads up in a queue, and the parallelism is gone.

The best pattern is not to touch shared state in the body at all: each worker keeps its own local total and merges it into the shared one once at the end. There is an overload with localInit and localFinally for that.
cards.code:
long total = 0;
Parallel.For(0, data.Length,
    () => 0L,                                    // localInit: a total per worker
    (i, state, local) => local + data[i],        // body: only the local sum
    local => Interlocked.Add(ref total, local)); // localFinally: merge once, atomically

cards.q: Which line loses increments?
cards.explain: count++ is a read, an add and a write. Two threads read the same value, both write +1, and one increment is lost. Use Interlocked.Increment(ref count) or local totals.

cards.title: Stopping, exceptions, Invoke
cards.body:
• ParallelLoopState.Stop() — stop as soon as possible;
  • ParallelLoopState.Break() — do not start iterations with higher indices, but finish all lower ones. Used to find the first match;
  • ParallelOptions: MaxDegreeOfParallelism and CancellationToken (on cancellation — OperationCanceledException);
  • an exception in an iteration: no new iterations start, running ones finish, and all errors arrive as one AggregateException from the Parallel.For call itself.

Parallel.Invoke runs several different actions and returns when all are done.

cards.q: You are looking for the element with the lowest index that matches a condition. What do you call in the iteration that found one?
options: state.Break()
state.Stop()
return from the lambda
Cancel() on your own CancellationTokenSource
cards.explain: Break guarantees that all iterations with lower indices will run: if one of them matches, you will not miss it. The lowest index Break was called from is in ParallelLoopResult.LowestBreakIteration.

wrong.1: Stop may leave lower-index iterations unexecuted — the element you found is not necessarily the first.
wrong.2: return ends only the current iteration; the loop goes on.

cards.title: PLINQ: AsParallel
cards.body:
PLINQ is parallel LINQ to Objects. AsParallel() turns a sequence into a ParallelQuery<T>, and the operators after it run on several threads.

  • The query is lazy, like regular LINQ: the work starts on foreach or ToList.
  • Order is not preserved. AsOrdered() restores the source order at the cost of buffering.
  • WithDegreeOfParallelism(n) — how many workers (by default as many as cores), WithCancellation(ct) — cancellation.
  • ForAll(action) — process results right on the worker threads, without merging them into one thread.
cards.code:
var hits = files
    .AsParallel()
    .WithDegreeOfParallelism(4)
    .Where(f => Hash(f) == target)   // computed on 4 threads
    .ToList();                       // results are merged, any order
cards.deep:
PLINQ analyzes the shape of the query and, for some combinations of operators, decides to run it sequentially if it thinks parallelism will not pay off. WithExecutionMode(ParallelExecutionMode.ForceParallelism) forces parallel execution.

WithMergeOptions controls how results are handed to the consumer: NotBuffered — one at a time right away, FullyBuffered — all at once at the end, AutoBuffered — in chunks (the default).

cards.q: What is guaranteed about the order of elements in r?
cards.code:
int[] r = Enumerable.Range(1, 8)
    .AsParallel()
    .Select(x => x * 10)
    .ToArray();
options: Nothing: without AsOrdered the order can be anything
Source order: ToArray restores it by itself
Source order: Range knows its indices in advance
Reverse: the last thread writes first
cards.explain: Without AsOrdered PLINQ promises no order, even if on a small example it often matches the source. If you need order, use AsParallel().AsOrdered().

cards.q: Spread heavy log parsing over 4 threads with PLINQ
cards.code:
var errors = lines
    .___()
    .___(4)
    .Where(l => Parse(l).IsError)
    .ToList();
cards.explain: AsParallel turns PLINQ on, WithDegreeOfParallelism limits the number of workers. MaxDegreeOfParallelism is a ParallelOptions property for the Parallel class, not a PLINQ operator.

cards.title: I/O: ForEachAsync, not ForEach
cards.body:
Parallel.For and Parallel.ForEach take a synchronous body — an Action<T>. Pass an async lambda there and the compiler turns it into an async void method (unit 5): there is no task, and the loop considers the iteration done as soon as the lambda reaches its first await. The loop returns while the downloads are still running, and their exceptions fly as from async void — into the context or straight into the pool, crashing the process.

For waiting there is Parallel.ForEachAsync (unit 5). Its mechanism: up to N worker tasks; each takes the next element from a shared enumerator, awaits the body and takes the next one. How it differs from Parallel.For:

  • The default limit. For Parallel.For, MaxDegreeOfParallelism defaults to −1 — no limit, as many threads as the pool gives. For ForEachAsync, without the setting N = Environment.ProcessorCount.
  • Waiting. Parallel.For holds the calling thread until the end. ForEachAsync returns a task, and while the bodies wait for I/O, threads are free.
  • Exceptions. Parallel.For throws AggregateException from the call itself. In ForEachAsync the first exception cancels the ct token the body receives; nobody takes new elements, the bodies already started finish, and the task completes with an error: await throws the body's exception.
cards.code:
// the body is Func<T, CancellationToken, ValueTask>: every iteration has a task
await Parallel.ForEachAsync(urls,
    new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 8 },   // without it — ProcessorCount
    async (url, ct) => await SaveAsync(url, ct));         // ct is cancelled on the first error
cards.deep: ForEachAsync collects all the bodies' exceptions in its task: task.Exception holds an AggregateException with all of them, and await, as usual, throws the first one. If your ParallelOptions.CancellationToken was cancelled, the task ends as Canceled: await throws OperationCanceledException, and body errors caused by that cancellation are treated as its consequence.

cards.q: Why does "all downloaded" print before everything is downloaded? Find the line.
cards.explain: Parallel.ForEach takes an Action<T>, and the async lambda becomes async void. Each iteration returns at its first await, and the loop considers it done. Errors from async void will also crash the process. For I/O, use await Parallel.ForEachAsync.

cards.title: When parallelism loses
cards.body:
• A cheap body. Partitioning, delegate calls and merging cost more than x * 2. A thousand such iterations are faster sequentially.
  • Shared state under a lock. Threads queue up behind the lock.
  • Memory-bound work. A simple pass over a huge array is limited by RAM bandwidth, not by the number of cores.
  • False sharing. The CPU moves data between memory and a core's cache not byte by byte but in cache lines — blocks of usually 64 bytes. To write to a line, a core must take it into exclusive ownership, and the copies of that line in other cores' caches become invalid. If threads write to different variables in the same line, the line bounces between cores on every write. There is no shared data in the code, yet the cores still wait for each other.
  • I/O inside. Pool threads just sit and wait. Here you need Parallel.ForEachAsync or WhenAll.

Measurement decides, not intuition: BenchmarkDotNet on real data.
cards.deep:
If you do need a shared array, spread the cells apart: give each thread its own element 64 bytes or more away (for example, new long[8 * 16] and index t * 16), or use a struct with [StructLayout(LayoutKind.Explicit, Size = 128)].

For a cheap body, slice the range coarsely: Partitioner.Create(0, n) hands out "from — to" pairs, and inside each one runs a plain for. One delegate call per chunk instead of per element: Parallel.ForEach(Partitioner.Create(0, n), r => { for (int i = r.Item1; i < r.Item2; i++) a[i] *= 2; });

cards.q: Where will spreading CPU work across cores (Parallel.For or PLINQ) actually give the speedup? Select all.
options: Computing SHA-256 for 10,000 large in-memory buffers
Multiplying each element of a 1000-int array by 2
Rendering a 4K frame pixel by pixel with a heavy formula on the CPU
Downloading 500 pages over HTTP
Adding to a shared counter under a lock in every iteration
cards.explain: Heavy independent CPU work speeds up. 1000 multiplications are cheaper than the overhead, and a shared lock lines threads up in a queue. HTTP through Parallel.ForEach formally gets faster, but at the cost of blocked pool threads: that is waiting, not computation — it needs Parallel.ForEachAsync.

cards.q: Match the tool to the job
pairs: An index loop with CPU work
Keep the source order in PLINQ
Atomically add to a shared variable

lessons.title: Timers, threads and cancellation
lessons.sub: Who holds a timer, who holds the process, and how to link cancellations

cards.title: Timers: who calls you and where
cards.body:
• System.Threading.Timer — calls the callback on a pool thread every period. If the callback takes longer than the period, the next one starts without waiting — callbacks overlap on different threads. Change reschedules, Timeout.Infinite turns it off.
  • System.Timers.Timer — a wrapper with an Elapsed event and AutoReset, also on the pool.
  • UI timers (DispatcherTimer, System.Windows.Forms.Timer) — the tick goes through the message queue on the UI thread. No overlap, but a long handler freezes the window.
cards.deep:
An exception from a System.Threading.Timer callback is an unhandled exception on a pool thread: the process crashes. System.Timers.Timer, per its documentation, swallows exceptions from Elapsed handlers — the error simply vanishes.

The runtime keeps timers in its own queues; a service thread tracks when they fire, and the callbacks go to the pool. Since .NET 8 there is TimeProvider: TimeProvider.System.CreateTimer(…) in code and a fake provider in tests — time can be "advanced" without real waiting.

cards.q: A System.Threading.Timer has a 1 s period, and the callback runs for 3 s. What happens?
options: Callbacks overlap: a second later the next one starts on another thread
The timer waits for the callback to end and shifts the next tick
Extra ticks are dropped; there is always one callback
The timer throws an overload exception
cards.explain: The timer does not know whether you are done. About three callbacks will run at once, and shared data in them must be protected. If you do not want overlap, start the timer as one-shot (period = Timeout.Infinite) and re-arm it at the end of the callback: Change(1000, Timeout.Infinite). A timer for async without overlap comes two cards later.

cards.title: Who holds the timer
cards.body:
A running timer is registered in a runtime queue, but the queue holds an internal part, not your Timer object. If nobody keeps a reference to the Timer, the garbage collector may collect it — the finalizer stops the timer, and the ticks silently end. The documentation says it plainly: keep a reference to the timer for as long as you need it.

The nasty part is that the bug comes and goes. If the timer is a local variable of a long method, in a Debug build the JIT extends its lifetime to the end of the method, and everything works. In Release the variable is dead right after its last use.

The flip side: while a timer is active, the queue holds the callback and everything it captured. A timer in a field of the object whose method it calls holds that object in a circle: queue → callback → object → timer. Such a timer will never be collected on its own — stop it with Dispose.
cards.deep: In .NET Core a timer is split into three objects: Timer → TimerHolder (with a finalizer) → TimerQueueTimer. The queue references only the last one. So an abandoned Timer and its holder become garbage, and the holder's finalizer closes the TimerQueueTimer — otherwise a forgotten timer would tick forever.

cards.q: What happens to the ticks?
options: They will stop soon
They go on forever: the timer sits in a runtime queue
They never start: a timer needs a dedicated thread
After each collection they come twice as often
cards.explain: After StartTicking returns, not a single reference to the Timer is left. A collection will collect it, and the finalizer stops the timer. The runtime queue holds only the internal part, not your object. The fix: keep the timer in a field and release it with Dispose.

cards.title: PeriodicTimer: a timer for async
cards.body:
PeriodicTimer (.NET 6) works without callbacks — as a loop with await WaitForNextTickAsync:

  • ticks do not overlap: the next iteration starts only when you come back to wait;
  • missed ticks do not pile up: if the work took three periods, at most one tick is pending, and the next wait completes immediately;
  • stopping — Dispose (the wait returns false) or a token (throws OperationCanceledException);
  • only one consumer may wait at a time.

.NET 8 added a Period property you can change on the fly, and a constructor that takes a TimeProvider.
cards.deep: Inside it is the same TimerQueueTimer. WaitForNextTickAsync returns a ValueTask<bool> over a reusable IValueTaskSource, so a tick creates no new task. That is also where the "one waiter" limit comes from: the timer has a single source.

cards.q: Sync once a minute without overlap
cards.explain: The loop sets the pace itself: while SyncAsync is running, a new tick will not start a second instance.

cards.title: Your own threads: Start, Join, background and foreground
cards.body:
You can create a thread by hand: new Thread(method) creates an OS thread, Start() starts it, and Join() blocks the calling thread until that thread finishes. Join(timeout) waits no longer than the timeout and returns false if the thread is still alive.

A process lives as long as at least one foreground thread is alive. Main has returned, but a new Thread(…) is still running — the process waits for it.

Background threads (IsBackground = true) do not hold the process. When the last foreground thread ends, the process exits, and background threads are cut off where they are: no exception, and finally does not run.

  • Background: all pool threads — so Task.Run, timer callbacks, continuations after await; the LongRunning thread.
  • Foreground: the main thread and new Thread by default.

You cannot kill a thread from outside. .NET Framework had Thread.Abort: it threw ThreadAbortException into another thread at an arbitrary point — an asynchronous exception that could land even between two lines that must go together (take a resource, enter the try). In .NET Core and .NET 5+ Thread.Abort throws PlatformNotSupportedException: foreign code can only be stopped cooperatively, for example with a cancellation token.
cards.deep:
For a clean shutdown, do not rely on a thread — give it a signal: in the .NET host that is BackgroundService and its stoppingToken, for the process — the AppDomain.ProcessExit event.

Thread.Abort had rules of its own: unlike cutting off a background thread, it did run finally blocks, and a catch could not swallow the exception — it was rethrown at the end of the catch until the thread called Thread.ResetAbort.

cards.q: A console app. Will done.txt appear?
options: No: the pool thread is background, the process exits first
Yes: the process waits for all unfinished tasks
Yes: Task.Run creates a foreground thread
Only in a Debug build
cards.explain: Main has returned, no foreground threads are left — the process exits, and the task is cut off during Sleep. You need to wait for it: await Task.Run(…) in an async Main.

cards.q: Now it is your own background thread, but Join follows Start. What happens?
options: done.txt appears after 2 s, then main end is printed
main end at once, and done.txt never appears: the background thread is cut off
main end at once, and done.txt after 2 s: Join makes the thread foreground
Does not compile: only foreground threads have Join
cards.explain: Join blocks Main until thread t finishes — background or not. Main waits 2 s, the thread writes the file and exits, and only then is main end printed. IsBackground matters only when the process is exiting while the thread is still running.

wrong.2: Join changes nothing about the thread itself: it just waits for it to end.

cards.title: Register: what to do at the moment of cancellation
cards.body:
token.Register(callback) subscribes a callback to cancellation. That is how you connect cancellation to APIs without tokens: close a socket, cancel a TaskCompletionSource.

  • The callback runs synchronously on the thread that called Cancel() — right inside Cancel.
  • If the token is already cancelled, the callback runs immediately, inside Register itself.
  • Cancel collects callback exceptions into an AggregateException after all of them have run.
  • Register returns a CancellationTokenRegistration. Do not release it, and the callback and everything it captured live as long as the token source.
cards.deep:
Disposing a registration waits if the callback is running right now on another thread: afterwards the callback is guaranteed to have finished. Hold a lock the callback needs and you get a deadlock. Unregister() (.NET Core 3.0) removes the subscription without waiting.

Register(cb, useSynchronizationContext: true) posts the callback to the context captured at registration. CancelAsync() (.NET 8) runs the callbacks off your thread and returns a task.

cards.q: What does the code print?
options: A, then B
B, then A
Only B
InvalidOperationException
cards.explain: The token is already cancelled, so Register runs the callback immediately and synchronously, before it returns. A late subscriber does not miss the cancellation.

cards.title: Linked tokens and CancelAfter
cards.body:
Often there are two reasons to cancel: the caller changed their mind, and your own timeout expired.

  • CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(a, b) — a new source that is cancelled when any parent is (or by itself);
  • CancelAfter(time) — cancel on an internal timer. Calling it again resets the deadline;
  • a linked source subscribes to its parents via Register, so it must be disposed. Otherwise a long-lived parent accumulates subscriptions.

Check who cancelled in a when filter.
cards.deep:
How a task becomes Canceled rather than Faulted. For an async method, any OperationCanceledException that escapes makes the task Canceled. For Task.Run(work, ct) — only if the exception carries that same ct and it is cancelled; otherwise Faulted. That is why ThrowIfCancellationRequested beats a manual throw: the exception carries the right token from the start.

TryReset() (.NET 6) returns a non-cancelled source to its initial state — for pooling. Since .NET 8 the constructor accepts a TimeProvider, and a timeout can be tested without real waiting.

cards.q: The service runs for weeks, and memory slowly grows. Which line is to blame?
cards.explain: The linked source subscribed to appStopping, which lives for the whole lifetime of the service. Without Dispose each subscription stays in its list together with the source. You need using var cts.

cards.q: Match the tool to what it gives you
pairs: A callback at the moment of cancellation
Cancellation for any of several reasons
The thread does not hold the process

lessons.title: Final: tasks without await
lessons.sub: ContinueWith, schedulers and the pool, Parallel, timers, threads and cancellation

cards.q: A WPF button handler, not inside any task. Where does Heavy() run?
options: On the pool: outside a task TaskScheduler.Current is Default
On the UI thread: StartNew takes the current SynchronizationContext
On the UI thread: StartNew without a scheduler takes Current
On a new dedicated thread: that is how StartNew works by default
cards.explain: Current is the scheduler of the running task, not the thread's context. A button handler is not a task, so Current is Default. The trap fires only when the code is already inside a task on a UI scheduler. It is safer not to guess and to write Task.Run.

cards.q: Which line throws TaskCanceledException whatever the outcome of LoadAsync?
cards.explain: Of the two continuations one is always skipped and moves to Canceled: on success it is log, on failure it is show. WhenAll with a cancelled task is cancelled too, and await throws TaskCanceledException.

cards.q: How does Task.Run(work) differ from Task.Factory.StartNew(work)? Select all.
options: Task.Run always goes to TaskScheduler.Default
Task.Run forbids attaching child tasks
Task.Run unwraps the Task<Task> from an async lambda
Task.Run allocates a dedicated thread for long work
Task.Run picks up the caller's cancellation token by itself
cards.explain: Task.Run = StartNew with DenyChildAttach, TaskScheduler.Default and Unwrap for async lambdas. Only LongRunning gives a dedicated thread, and Task.Run uses only a token passed to it explicitly.

cards.q: Inside Task.Run a library creates a task with AttachedToParent and throws from it. What does await on your task see?
options: Nothing: the child did not attach, its error stays in its own task
An AggregateException with the child's error
Your task waits for the child and completes together with it
InvalidOperationException: attaching is forbidden
cards.explain: DenyChildAttach on the Task.Run task silently turns the child into an independent task. No waiting, no foreign exceptions. The child's error is the concern of whoever created it.

cards.q: You need a report in the source row order, but the heavy formula should run on all cores. What do you add?
options: .AsOrdered()
.WithDegreeOfParallelism(1)
.OrderBy(r => r)
Nothing: ToList preserves order
cards.explain: AsOrdered makes PLINQ return results in the source order while computing them in parallel. WithDegreeOfParallelism(1) kills the parallelism, and OrderBy sorts by value, not by position.

cards.q: Each thread writes only to its own hits cell, there is no race, and the check is cheap. Yet on 8 cores the loop is hardly faster than on one. Why?
options: The cells share a cache line, and it bounces between cores on every write
hits[t]++ is not atomic, and threads wait for each other on it
Parallel.For runs iterations one by one when there are no more of them than cores
Parallel.For takes only 2 threads by default
cards.explain: Eight longs are 64 bytes, one or two cache lines. To write, a core takes the line into exclusive ownership, and the copies in the other cores become invalid. That is false sharing. The cure is a local counter in the body and a single write to hits[t] at the end.

wrong.1: Non-atomicity is dangerous when several threads write to the same cell. Here each has its own — there is nothing to lose.

cards.q: UploadAsync throws HttpRequestException on the fifth url. What happens?
cards.code:
await Parallel.ForEachAsync(urls,
    async (url, ct) => await UploadAsync(url, ct));
options: ct is cancelled, no new urls are taken, uploads already started finish, and await throws HttpRequestException
The remaining urls are processed, and at the end await throws an AggregateException with all the errors
The process crashes: the body's exception went to a pool thread, as with async void
All started uploads are cut off on the spot, and await returns without an error
cards.explain: The ForEachAsync body returns a ValueTask, so the exception lands in a task, not in the pool. The first error cancels the shared ct token: the worker tasks stop taking elements, and bodies already started finish (or exit via ct). The ForEachAsync task completes with an error, and await throws the body's exception.

wrong.2: That is what an async lambda in Parallel.ForEach would do. The ForEachAsync body is a function with a task, not async void.

cards.q: A PeriodicTimer has a 5 s period, and the work in the loop takes 8 s. How do the runs go?
options: Back to back: one missed tick is pending, extra ones do not pile up
Overlapping: a new instance starts every 5 s
Every 10 s: a missed tick postpones the next one
Missed ticks accumulate, and the loop catches up on them
cards.explain: While the work runs, the timer remembers at most one tick. The next wait completes immediately, and the work takes 8 s again. No overlap: a new iteration does not start until you return to WaitForNextTickAsync.

cards.q: A background thread (IsBackground = true) is writing a file in try/finally when Main ends. What about finally?
options: It does not run: the runtime stops background threads without an exception
It runs: finally always runs
It runs: on exit a ThreadAbortException is raised in the thread
The process waits until the background thread finishes the file
cards.explain: Background threads do not hold the process. When the last foreground thread ends, they are cut off where they are, and finally does not run. For a clean exit — a cancellation token and waiting for the work.

cards.q: Cancel the request if the caller cancels or 10 seconds pass, and leave no subscription on someone else's token
cards.explain: The linked source is cancelled for either reason, CancelAfter adds the timeout, and using removes the subscription on ct when the method ends.

cards.q: Match them and test yourself on the whole unit
pairs: A task that waits for the inner task
A dedicated thread for blocking work
Finish the iterations with lower indices
A continuation without the scheduler queue
A callback on the thread that called Cancel

units.title: Synchronization in depth
units.blurb: The memory model and volatile, Interlocked and the CAS loop, spinning vs kernel objects, Monitor and the Lock type, Lazy<T> and concurrent collections. The course final.

lessons.title: The memory model and volatile
lessons.sub: Which reorderings are possible, x64 vs ARM64, Volatile.Read/Write

cards.title: Order in code is not order in memory
cards.body:
In the unit on tasks without await the race was easy to picture: count++ is three steps (read, add, write), and two threads interleave them. There is a subtler problem. Even without shared counters, another thread can see your writes in a different order than you wrote them.

Three parties change the order:

  • the C# compiler — almost never, it does little optimization;
  • the JIT — merges reads, keeps a field in a register, reorders independent operations;
  • the CPU — executes instructions out of order and queues writes in a store buffer before they reach the cache.

All three promise one thing: within one thread the result is as if the code ran strictly in order. They promise nothing about other threads — except what the rules of the memory model guarantee.

cards.title: The loop that never stops
cards.body:
A classic. One thread spins until a flag is raised, another thread raises it.

The JIT sees that nothing inside the loop changes _stop. So it may read it once before the loop and keep testing a register. For a single thread that is a fair optimization. For two threads it is an endless loop: the other thread did write to memory, but this thread never looks at memory again.

Atomicity has nothing to do with it: a bool is written and read as a whole. The problem is visibility — the read simply is not there. The fix is to read through Volatile.Read(ref _stop) or to put the volatile keyword on the field: the JIT is not allowed to merge such a read or hoist it out of the loop. How they work comes later in this lesson.
cards.deep:
In a Debug build and at tier 0 of tiered compilation the JIT barely optimizes, and the code "works". Once a hot method is recompiled at tier 1 (or replaced mid-loop through OSR, on-stack replacement), the read is hoisted out of the loop and the program hangs. That is why the bug shows up "only in Release and only sometimes".

The memory model spec in the dotnet/runtime repository allows this explicitly: adjacent ordinary reads of the same location can be coalesced into one.

cards.q: Release build, Run() spins in one thread, a second later another thread calls Stop(). What happens?
options: It may hang forever: the read of _stop was hoisted out of the loop
It always prints "done": a bool is written atomically
It throws InvalidOperationException
It prints "done", but only after a scheduler quantum
cards.explain: Atomicity is not the issue: writing a bool is indeed indivisible. The problem is visibility — the Run thread no longer reads the field from memory, and t.Join() waits forever. The fix is Volatile.Read(ref _stop) or volatile on the field.

wrong.1: Atomic means "you will not read half a value". It does not promise the read happens at all.

cards.title: Four reorderings: x64 vs ARM64
cards.body:
Take two operations on different memory locations. The pairs are: read→read, read→write, write→write, write→read. Which of them the CPU can "swap" as seen from another core depends on the architecture.

  • x64 has a strong model (TSO). Only one reordering is visible: a write followed by a read of another location. The write is still sitting in the buffer while the read already went to the cache.
  • ARM64 has a weak model. All four are possible. That is Apple M-series, Graviton, Ampere, phones.

Hence a nasty class of bugs: code ran for years on x64 servers, and after moving to ARM64 it starts seeing "impossible" states once a day. And the JIT may reorder on its own, on any architecture.
cards.deep: TSO is total store order: all cores see writes in a single common order, and a core reads its own not-yet-flushed writes from the buffer (store forwarding). That is why write→read is the only hardware reordering on x64, and only a full fence fixes it: the mfence instruction or any lock-prefixed instruction.

cards.q: Which reordering of operations on different locations can an x64 CPU show to another core?
options: A write, then a read: the read overtakes the write
Two writes swap places
Two reads swap places
A read, then a write: the write overtakes the read
cards.explain: The write waits in the store buffer while the next read of another location has already executed. x64 does not do the other three — ARM64 does all four.

cards.title: Publishing through a flag
cards.body:
Thread A prepares data and raises a flag. Thread B sees the flag and reads the data. On ARM64, B can see _ready == true but a stale _data == 0: A's writes became visible in reverse order, or B's reads executed in reverse order.

Two promises are needed:

  • the flag write is a release: everything A did before it becomes visible no later than the flag;
  • the flag read is an acquire: everything B does after it will not run earlier.

These are the two methods of the static Volatile class: Volatile.Write(ref field, value) is a write with release, Volatile.Read(ref field) is a read with acquire. There are overloads for all primitive types and references.

cards.q: Fix the loop from the start of the lesson without changing the field declaration
cards.explain: Volatile.Read cannot be merged with neighboring reads or hoisted out of the loop — the thread looks at memory every time. Volatile.Write makes the write a release. Load and Store are what memory model descriptions and other languages call these operations, but the Volatile class has no methods with those names.

cards.title: The volatile keyword and what it does not give you
cards.body:
volatile on a field turns every read into Volatile.Read and every write into Volatile.Write. Convenient, but it is easy to forget that the promises end there:

  • no atomicity for compound operations: _count++ on a volatile field is still three steps, increments still get lost;
  • no write→read ordering: a release write and a following acquire read of another location can still swap.

The second one breaks "raise my flag, check the other flag" algorithms. You need a full fence — an operation that no read and no write can cross in either direction. That is Interlocked.Exchange instead of a plain write, or an explicit fence between the lines: Interlocked.MemoryBarrier(), also available as Thread.MemoryBarrier().

And a type restriction: you cannot put volatile on long or double — error CS0677, because on a 32-bit platform writing them is not atomic. For such fields use Volatile.Read and Volatile.Write: they do have overloads for long and double.
cards.deep:
volatile is allowed on references, pointers, integers up to 32 bits, bool, char, float, IntPtr/nint and enums based on them. Per the memory model spec, Volatile.Read(ref long) is atomic even on 32 bits.

The old Thread.VolatileRead/VolatileWrite from .NET Framework issued a full fence — they are slower and no longer needed: the Volatile class arrived in .NET Framework 4.5.

cards.q: In the code above both fields are volatile and there is no fence. Can you get r1 == 0 and r2 == 0?
options: Yes: volatile does not stop a read from overtaking an earlier write
No: volatile forbids all reorderings
Only on ARM64, never on x64
No, if the threads run on different cores
cards.explain: A release write holds back what came before it, an acquire read holds back what comes after it. The pair "write, then read" is covered by neither. On x64 it is exactly the one reordering the hardware does. A full fence between the lines in both threads (Interlocked.Exchange instead of the write, or Interlocked.MemoryBarrier) rules this outcome out.

wrong.2: The opposite: write→read is exactly what x64 reorders by itself through the store buffer.

cards.title: What the .NET memory model guarantees
cards.body:
ECMA-335 promises little. The real runtime (CoreCLR) gives more, and it is written down in the memory model spec in dotnet/runtime:

  • aligned reads and writes up to pointer size are atomic — you never see half a value;
  • a volatile read is an acquire, a volatile write is a release;
  • storing an object reference to a shared location is a release: whoever reads the reference sees the object's fields initialized, without an extra fence;
  • ordering honors data dependency: a read through a reference does not happen before reading the reference itself;
  • Interlocked, Thread.MemoryBarrier and entering/leaving a lock are fences (Interlocked and MemoryBarrier are full ones).

The cost differs by CPU. On x64 a volatile read or write is a plain mov instruction: the hardware already gives acquire and release, and the constraint applies only to the JIT — do not merge, do not reorder. On ARM64 the JIT emits dedicated ldar/stlr instructions (load-acquire and store-release) or a dmb barrier. A full fence costs more everywhere: on x64 it is a lock-prefixed instruction or mfence.
cards.deep:
Exactly which instructions the JIT emits on ARM64 depends on its version and the spot in the code: ldar/stlr or a dmb barrier. A full fence on ARM64 is dmb ish.

Note: the "storing a reference is a release" guarantee does not order two independent ordinary writes. If order matters, say so explicitly with Volatile.

cards.title: Do you need volatile across await?
cards.body:
No. You know from the "Under the hood" unit that the locals of an async method are fields of the state machine, and the continuation after await may run on another thread. So one thread writes memory and another reads it. Still, everything written before await is visible after it.

The reason is the path the continuation takes to the other thread. The task completes by changing its state with Interlocked.CompareExchange, the continuation is put into the pool queue with atomic operations, and the pool thread takes it from the queue atomically too. These are full fences, and they order everything that came before them.

volatile, Volatile and Interlocked are for fields that two threads use at the same time: a stop flag, a counter, publishing an object. When the parts of one chain run in turn through await, the task hands the data over by itself.

cards.q: A method writes _total, then does await SaveAsync(), then reads _total. Another pool thread runs the continuation, and nobody else touches _total. Does _total need volatile?
options: No: completing the task and queuing the continuation are full fences
Yes: the other thread may read a stale value from its core's cache
Yes, but only on ARM64
You need a lock around the read after await
cards.explain: One thread wrote, another read — but strictly in turn, with the atomic operations of Task and the pool queue in between. Everything written before await is visible after it. volatile is needed when different threads read and write a field at the same time.

wrong.1: Stale values do not come from "its own cache" — the hardware keeps core caches coherent — but from reordering and merging. On the continuation's path the fences rule those out.

cards.q: What is true about volatile in C#? Select all.
options: A long field cannot be declared volatile
_count++ on a volatile field becomes atomic
A read of a volatile field cannot be hoisted out of a loop
A volatile write and a following volatile read of another field can swap places
On x64 every volatile read is a separate fence instruction
cards.explain: long is forbidden (CS0677). ++ is still three steps — you need Interlocked. Hoisting is not allowed: every volatile read is real. The write→read pair is not ordered. On x64 a volatile read is a plain mov, the constraints apply to the JIT only.

cards.q: Match the operation with what it promises
pairs: Acquire: later operations will not move earlier
Release: earlier operations will not move later
A full fence in both directions
May be merged with a neighbor and hoisted out of a loop
Storing a reference to a new object
The reader sees the fields initialized

lessons.title: Interlocked and the CAS loop
lessons.sub: Atomic instructions, CompareExchange and lock-free updates

cards.title: What happens inside the CPU
cards.body:
You have already met Interlocked.Increment. Now — how it works. The JIT turns the call not into a method call but straight into an atomic instruction:

  • x64 — a lock-prefixed instruction: lock xadd for Add/Increment (or lock add when the result is unused), lock cmpxchg for CompareExchange, xchg for Exchange;
  • ARM64 — LSE atomic instructions (ldaddal, casal) if the CPU supports them, otherwise a loop of "exclusive load — conditional store".

The core takes the cache line into exclusive ownership, does the read-modify-write, and nobody can squeeze in between. It is also a full fence: no operation jumps over it in either direction.

cards.title: Cost: cheap until it gets crowded
cards.body:
Without contention an atomic operation costs on the order of a few to tens of nanoseconds — more than a plain ++, but far less than a trip into the kernel.

Under contention the picture changes. To write, a core needs the line in exclusive ownership. Sixteen threads hammering one counter make the line bounce between the cores' caches. Every operation waits until the line is handed over. Add threads — it gets slower.

The cure is the same as for false sharing in the unit on tasks without await: give each thread its own counter and sum at the end. That is what localInit and localFinally of Parallel.For do: a thread accumulates its total in a local variable and merges it into the shared one once, through Interlocked.Add.

cards.q: An x64 server, 16 threads call Interlocked.Increment on one field in a loop. Why is it slower than a single thread?
options: The cache line holding the counter bounces between cores, every operation waits for it
Interlocked takes a lock on an object, threads queue up
Under contention Interlocked falls back to the OS kernel
Interlocked.Increment retries until it wins
cards.explain: The atomic instruction blocks nothing and never enters the kernel. It simply cannot start until the core gets the line in exclusive ownership. The bottleneck is the cache coherence protocol.

wrong.1: There is no object and no Monitor here: it is a single CPU instruction.
wrong.3: Retries belong to the CAS loop you write yourself. Increment on x64 is a single atomic instruction, and it always succeeds.

cards.title: What Interlocked methods return
cards.body:
A common mistake is mixing up what comes back: the new value or the old one.

  • Increment, Decrement, Add — the new value;
  • Exchange — the old one: you write yours and get what was there;
  • CompareExchange — the old one, always, whether the swap happened or not;
  • And, Or (.NET 5+) — the old one;
  • Read(ref long) — an atomic read of a 64-bit number. It is needed only in a 32-bit process: there a long read is two instructions, and without Interlocked.Read you can get a "torn" value — the old half and the new half. In a 64-bit process an aligned long read is atomic anyway (lesson 1).
cards.code:
int n = 5;
Interlocked.Add(ref n, 3);        // returns 8
Interlocked.Exchange(ref n, 0);   // returns 8, n == 0
Interlocked.Or(ref n, 0b100);     // returns 0, n == 4
cards.deep:
Interlocked.Read exists only for long/ulong. Other types up to pointer size do not need it: their aligned reads are atomic everywhere.

The set of overloads keeps growing: in .NET 9 Exchange and CompareExchange got versions for byte and short. For reference types there are the generic Exchange<T> and CompareExchange<T>.

cards.q: Match the call (n was 10) with what it returns

cards.title: CompareExchange — the brick of lock-free code
cards.body:
CompareExchange(ref location, value, comparand) atomically does: "if location holds comparand, write value". It returns what was in location before the call. This is CAS — compare-and-swap.

How to tell the swap succeeded: you got back exactly what you expected (comparand).

The trap is argument order: the new value first, then the expected one. Other languages and algorithm write-ups often do it the other way round.

cards.title: The CAS loop: read, compute, try
cards.body:
Interlocked can add, but it cannot "write the maximum". Any such update follows one pattern:

  • read the current value;
  • compute the new value from the old one;
  • CAS: write the new value if the old one has not changed;
  • failed — someone got there first; take what they wrote and repeat.

No lock, nobody sleeps. A thread that loses the race just redoes the computation with fresh data.

cards.q: Put the steps of one CAS loop iteration in order
items: Read the current value
Compute the new value from what you read
Call CompareExchange with what you read as the comparand
Compare the result with what you read
Not equal — take the returned value and repeat
cards.explain: The key is step 4: CompareExchange returns what was actually there. Equal to the expected value — the write went through. Not equal — that is your fresh value, no need to re-read the field.

cards.q: A lock-free stack. Under contention it loses items. Which line should be inside the loop but is outside?
cards.explain: After a lost attempt head is updated, but node.Next still points at the old top. The next CAS successfully puts node on top — and the chain skips the items other threads pushed in between. The node's link must be recomputed on every iteration: the "compute the new value" step belongs inside the loop.

cards.title: Lock-free does not mean wait-free
cards.body:
